Anatomy & Physiology.q: A student is describing the tissues that attach a tooth to its socket. Which statement correctly describes the periodontal ligament?
o: It is a fibrous connective tissue
It is a mineralised hard tissue
It is a specialised form of enamel
It is an avascular layer with no blood supply
It is the outermost layer of dentine
Anatomy & Physiology.w: The periodontal ligament is a fibrous connective tissue, not a hard tissue.

n.1: Cementum and bone are mineralised; the ligament between them is not.
n.2: Enamel covers the crown and has no role in attachment.
n.3: The ligament is well supplied with blood vessels and nerves.
n.4: Dentine lies beneath enamel and cementum, not in the socket.

Anatomy & Physiology.q: A patient presents with inflammation of the tissue surrounding the teeth within the oral cavity. Which structure is most likely affected?
Anatomy & Physiology.w: The gingiva (gums) surround the teeth and are commonly affected by inflammation such as gingivitis.

n.2: The hard palate forms the roof of the mouth, not surrounding teeth.
n.4: The tongue is involved in taste and movement, not surrounding teeth.
n.0: Buccal mucosa lines the cheeks, not directly surrounding teeth.
n.3: The soft palate is located posteriorly in the roof of the mouth.

Anatomy & Physiology.q: A dentist asks the nurse to retract the patient's tongue to examine the structure that connects it to the floor of the mouth. What is the best action?
Anatomy & Physiology.w: Retracting the tongue allows clear visualization of the lingual frenulum.

n.4: The uvula is located at the soft palate.
n.3: The soft palate is posterior and not under the tongue.
n.1: Gingiva is around the teeth, not under the tongue.
n.0: Buccal mucosa is in the cheeks.

Anatomy & Physiology.q: A patient presents with plaque accumulation primarily on the inner surfaces of their lower incisors. Which tooth surface is most affected?
Anatomy & Physiology.w: The lingual surface refers to the inner surface of anterior teeth facing the tongue, where plaque commonly accumulates in lower incisors.

n.1: The labial surface is the outer surface facing the lips.
n.4: Occlusal surfaces are found on posterior teeth, not incisors.
n.3: Mesial refers to the surface toward the midline, not the inner surface.
n.0: Distal refers to the surface away from the midline.

Anatomy & Physiology.q: A patient complains of sensitivity when brushing the outer surface of their front teeth. Which surface is most likely affected?
Anatomy & Physiology.w: The labial surface is the outer surface of anterior teeth facing the lips.

n.2: Lingual surfaces face the tongue.
n.3: Mesial surfaces are between teeth.
n.0: Distal surfaces are away from the midline.
n.4: Occlusal surfaces are not present on anterior teeth.

Anatomy & Physiology.q: A dentist instructs a patient to improve cleaning between adjacent teeth to prevent caries formation. Which surfaces are most relevant?
Anatomy & Physiology.w: Mesial and distal surfaces are proximal surfaces where adjacent teeth contact and plaque often accumulates.

n.2: Labial and lingual surfaces are external surfaces, not between teeth.
n.4: Occlusal surfaces are chewing surfaces, not contact points.
n.0: Buccal and occlusal surfaces are not proximal contact areas.
n.1: Incisal and buccal surfaces are not adjacent contact areas.

Anatomy & Physiology.q: A patient complains of persistent toothache and swelling. Examination suggests inflammation within the central part of the tooth. Which structure is affected?
Anatomy & Physiology.w: The pulp chamber contains nerves and blood vessels and is the site of inflammation in pulpitis.

n.2: Enamel does not contain nerves or blood supply.
n.1: Dentine transmits sensation but is not the origin of inflammation.
n.0: Cementum protects the root but is not involved in pulp inflammation.
n.3: The periodontal ligament supports the tooth but is not the central tissue affected.

Anatomy & Physiology.q: A clinician observes wear facets on the chewing surfaces of posterior teeth. What is the correct term for these surfaces?
Anatomy & Physiology.w: Occlusal surfaces are the chewing surfaces where wear facets commonly occur.

n.0: Buccal surfaces face the cheeks.
n.2: Lingual surfaces face the tongue.
n.3: Mesial surfaces are toward the midline.
n.1: Distal surfaces are away from the midline.

Anatomy & Physiology.q: A patient presents with gingivitis. Which structure is primarily inflamed?
Anatomy & Physiology.w: Gingivitis is inflammation of the gingival tissues.

n.2: Enamel is not inflamed.
n.1: Dentine is not soft tissue.
n.4: Pulp inflammation is pulpitis.
n.0: Bone inflammation is not gingivitis.

Anatomy & Physiology.q: A dentist identifies tooth 14 for treatment. What is the best action for the dental nurse?
o: Prepare for lower left first premolar treatment
Prepare for lower right first premolar treatment
Prepare for upper left first premolar treatment
Prepare for upper right first premolar treatment
Prepare for upper right second premolar treatment
Anatomy & Physiology.w: Tooth 14 is in quadrant 1 (upper right) and position 4 (first premolar).

n.2: Upper left first premolar would be 24.
n.1: Lower right first premolar would be 44.
n.4: Upper right second premolar would be 15.
n.0: Lower left first premolar would be 34.

Anatomy & Physiology.q: Based on the image provided, which structure is the outermost protective layer of the crown?
Anatomy & Physiology.w: Enamel is the highly mineralised outer layer of the crown that provides protection.

n.1: Dentine lies beneath enamel and is not the outermost layer.
n.4: The pulp chamber is internal.
n.0: Cementum covers the root, not the crown.
n.3: The periodontal ligament supports the tooth within bone.

Anatomy & Physiology.q: Which surface of the tooth shown in the image would be most prone to plaque accumulation due to pits and fissures?
Anatomy & Physiology.w: The occlusal surface contains pits and fissures where plaque easily accumulates.

n.0: Buccal surfaces are smoother.
n.2: Lingual surfaces generally lack deep fissures.
n.3: Mesial surfaces are contact areas.
n.1: Distal surfaces are also contact areas.

Anatomy & Physiology.q: A dentist asks you to identify tooth 47. Which tooth is this?
Anatomy & Physiology.w: Quadrant 4 is lower right, and tooth 7 is the second molar, so 47 is the lower right second molar.

n.0: Lower left second molar would be 37.
n.4: Upper right second molar would be 17.
n.3: Upper left second molar would be 27.
n.1: Lower right first molar would be 46.

Anatomy & Physiology.q: A patient is referred for treatment of tooth 41. Which tooth should the nurse prepare for?
Anatomy & Physiology.w: Quadrant 4 is lower right, and tooth 1 is the central incisor.

n.0: Lower left central incisor would be 31.
n.4: Upper right central incisor would be 11.
n.2: Lower right lateral incisor would be 42.
n.3: Upper left central incisor would be 21.

Anatomy & Physiology.q: A patient requires extraction of tooth 22. Which tooth is this?
Anatomy & Physiology.w: Quadrant 2 is upper left, and tooth 2 is the lateral incisor.

n.2: Central incisor in quadrant 2 would be 21.
n.4: Upper right lateral incisor would be 12.
n.0: Lower left lateral incisor would be 32.
n.1: Upper left canine would be 23.

Anatomy & Physiology.q: A dentist asks you to chart tooth 31. Which tooth is this referring to?
Anatomy & Physiology.w: Quadrant 3 is lower left, and tooth 1 is the central incisor, so 31 is the lower left central incisor.

n.2: Lower right central incisor would be 41.
n.3: Upper left central incisor would be 21.
n.4: Upper right central incisor would be 11.
n.1: Lower left lateral incisor would be 32.

Anatomy & Physiology.q: During polishing, a dental nurse is instructed to focus on the surfaces facing the cheeks on upper molars. Which surfaces are these?
Anatomy & Physiology.w: Buccal surfaces are those facing the cheeks on posterior teeth.

n.2: Lingual surfaces face the tongue.
n.4: Palatal surfaces refer specifically to upper teeth facing the palate, not cheeks.
n.3: Mesial surfaces are toward the midline.
n.1: Distal surfaces are away from the midline.

Anatomy & Physiology.q: Based on the image provided, which tooth corresponds to FDI number 36?
Anatomy & Physiology.w: Quadrant 3 is lower left and tooth 6 is the first molar, so 36 is the lower left first molar.

n.2: Lower right first molar would be 46.
n.3: Upper left first molar would be 26.
n.4: Upper right first molar would be 16.
n.1: Lower left second molar would be 37.

Anatomy & Physiology.q: A dental nurse is revising the major salivary glands. Where does the submandibular duct open into the mouth?
o: In the cheek opposite the upper second molar
In the floor of the mouth beside the lingual frenum
In the lower labial sulcus below the incisors
On the dorsum of the tongue near the midline
Through small openings across the hard palate
Anatomy & Physiology.w: The submandibular duct opens under the tongue, not opposite the upper molars, which is the parotid duct location.

n.0: That is where the parotid duct opens.
n.2: Only minor labial glands open here.
n.3: No major salivary duct opens on the tongue's upper surface.
n.4: Those are minor palatal glands, not the submandibular duct.

Anatomy & Physiology.q: A dental nurse is recording findings for the upper right first molar using the FDI system. Which tooth number should be recorded?
Anatomy & Physiology.w: In the FDI system, quadrant 1 is upper right and the first molar is tooth 6, giving 16.

n.2: 26 refers to the upper left first molar.
n.3: 36 refers to the lower left first molar.
n.4: 46 refers to the lower right first molar.
n.0: 15 refers to the upper right second premolar.

Anatomy & Physiology.q: During examination, the dentist identifies a ridge of tissue that supports the teeth sockets. Which structure is this?
Anatomy & Physiology.w: The alveolar ridge contains the tooth sockets and supports the teeth.

n.1: A bony ridge on the outer surface of the mandible, not the tooth-bearing ridge.
n.2: Runs along the inner surface of the mandible and gives muscle attachment.
n.3: Ridges of the hard palate, unrelated to the sockets.
n.4: Soft tissue behind the last lower molar.

Anatomy & Physiology.q: A dental nurse is asked to identify the part of the tooth visible above the gum line. What is the correct term?
Anatomy & Physiology.w: The crown is the visible portion of the tooth above the gingiva.

n.3: The root is below the gum line.
n.2: The pulp is internal.
n.1: The ligament supports the tooth.
n.4: The socket is part of bone.

Anatomy & Physiology.q: The dentist indicates the upper left third molar while charting an adult patient. Which FDI number should the dental nurse record?
Anatomy & Physiology.w: Tooth 28 correctly represents the upper left third molar, so there is no error.

n.0: 18 is the upper right third molar.
n.1: 27 is the upper left second molar.
n.3: 38 is the lower left third molar.
n.4: 48 is the lower right third molar.

Anatomy & Physiology.q: A patient reports that food tastes different following an injury to the mouth. Which oral cavity structure is primarily responsible for housing taste buds and aiding in speech and mastication?
Anatomy & Physiology.w: The tongue contains taste buds and plays a key role in speech and mastication.

n.3: The hard palate forms the roof of the mouth.
n.2: Gingiva supports teeth but does not contain taste buds.
n.1: Buccal mucosa lines the cheeks.
n.0: The alveolar ridge supports teeth.

Anatomy & Physiology.q: A dental nurse is charting a lower premolar during an examination. Which term describes the chewing surface of that tooth?
Anatomy & Physiology.w: Premolars have occlusal surfaces, not incisal surfaces, which are found on anterior teeth.

n.0: The buccal surface faces the cheek, not the opposing tooth.
n.1: Distal describes the surface furthest from the midline.
n.2: Incisal is the biting edge of anterior teeth only.
n.4: Palatal surfaces face the palate and are found in the upper arch.

Anatomy & Physiology.q: A dental nurse is assisting during a restoration of a molar where the chewing surface is being treated. Which surface is the dentist working on?
Anatomy & Physiology.w: The occlusal surface is the chewing surface of posterior teeth such as molars and premolars.

n.0: The buccal surface faces the cheeks.
n.2: The lingual surface faces the tongue.
n.3: Mesial refers to the surface toward the midline.
n.1: Incisal surfaces are found on anterior teeth.

Anatomy & Physiology.q: A patient asks why their teeth can withstand years of chewing. Which structure provides the primary protective barrier against mechanical damage to the tooth?
Anatomy & Physiology.w: Enamel is the hardest substance in the body and protects against wear.

n.4: Pulp is soft tissue.
n.1: Dentine supports but is less mineralised.
n.0: Cementum covers roots.
n.3: The periodontal ligament supports but does not protect.

Anatomy & Physiology.q: A patient attends after chipping a front tooth on a glass bottle. Which surface of an anterior tooth is primarily involved when a patient chips the biting edge of an incisor?
Anatomy & Physiology.w: The incisal edge is the cutting edge of anterior teeth and is the part most likely to chip.

n.2: The labial surface is the outer front surface.
n.3: The lingual surface is the inner surface.
n.4: Mesial refers to the side toward the midline.
n.0: Distal refers to the side away from the midline.

Anatomy & Physiology.q: Based on the image provided, which surface of the molar shows the cusps and fissures?
Anatomy & Physiology.w: The occlusal surface displays cusps and fissures used for chewing.

n.0: Buccal surfaces do not show cusps and fissures in detail.
n.2: Lingual surfaces are smoother and do not show full occlusal anatomy.
n.3: Mesial surfaces are contact surfaces, not functional chewing surfaces.
n.1: Distal surfaces are also contact surfaces.

Anatomy & Physiology.q: A patient complains of a persistently dry mouth between meals. Which salivary gland contributes the greatest proportion of resting saliva in the oral cavity?
Anatomy & Physiology.w: The submandibular gland produces the majority of resting saliva.

n.2: The parotid gland contributes mainly during stimulation.
n.3: The sublingual gland produces a smaller proportion of saliva.
n.1: Minor salivary glands contribute only small amounts.
n.0: Labial glands are minor contributors.

Anatomy & Physiology.q: A dental nurse is asked to assist in examining a duct opening located opposite the upper second molar. Which gland does this duct belong to?
Anatomy & Physiology.w: The parotid duct (Stensen’s duct) opens opposite the upper second molar.

n.4: The submandibular duct opens under the tongue.
n.3: The sublingual gland has multiple small ducts under the tongue.
n.1: Palatal glands are minor glands without this duct location.
n.0: Buccal glands are minor glands and do not have a major duct opening here.

Anatomy & Physiology.q: Based on the image provided, which quadrant contains tooth 24 in the FDI system?
Anatomy & Physiology.w: Quadrant 2 represents the upper left in the FDI system, so tooth 24 is located there.

n.4: Upper right corresponds to quadrant 1.
n.0: Lower left corresponds to quadrant 3.
n.1: Lower right corresponds to quadrant 4.
n.2: Primary teeth use quadrants 5–8, not 2.

Anatomy & Physiology.q: Which surface of a maxillary incisor faces the palate?
Anatomy & Physiology.w: The lingual surface of maxillary incisors faces the palate.

n.1: Labial surfaces face the lips.
n.0: Buccal surfaces apply to posterior teeth.
n.4: Occlusal surfaces are not present on incisors.
n.3: Mesial surfaces are toward the midline.

Anatomy & Physiology.q: A dental nurse notices a patient consistently misses cleaning the surfaces facing the tongue. What advice should be given?
o: Advise using a mouthwash after brushing
Increase brushing time on the buccal surfaces
Recommend an interdental brush for the front teeth
Suggest a whitening toothpaste for better coverage
Anatomy & Physiology.w: Lingual surfaces face the tongue and require effective brushing.

n.0: A useful adjunct, but it does not remove plaque from surfaces the brush is missing.
n.2: Spends more effort on the surfaces already being cleaned well.
n.3: Cleans between teeth rather than the tongue-facing surfaces being missed.
n.4: Toothpaste choice does not change which surfaces the brush reaches.

Anatomy & Physiology.q: A dental nurse is revising the structure of the dental tissues. Which statement correctly describes enamel?
o: It contains blood vessels that supply nutrients
It contains nerve endings that transmit sensation
It contains no living cells once it has formed
It contains odontoblast processes throughout its depth
It is renewed continuously by cells at its surface
Anatomy & Physiology.w: Enamel is non-vital and does not contain living cells.

n.0: Enamel is avascular; only the pulp carries blood vessels.
n.1: Enamel has no nerve supply; sensation comes from the pulp via dentine.
n.3: Odontoblast processes lie in dentinal tubules, not in enamel.
n.4: Ameloblasts are lost when the tooth erupts, so enamel cannot be replaced.

Anatomy & Physiology.q: A dental nurse is explaining tooth structure to a student on placement. Which sequence correctly describes the layers from the outer crown to the centre of the tooth?
Anatomy & Physiology.w: The correct sequence is enamel (outer), dentine (middle), and pulp (centre).

n.1: Dentine is not outermost.
n.4: Pulp is central, not outer.
n.3: Pulp is not between enamel and dentine.
n.0: Cementum is not part of the crown.

Anatomy & Physiology.q: A patient presents with exposed root surfaces due to recession. What is the best action to reduce sensitivity?
Anatomy & Physiology.w: Desensitising agents help block dentinal tubules and reduce sensitivity.

n.3: Enamel polishing does not address exposed roots.
n.4: Removing dentine worsens sensitivity.
n.1: Extraction is unnecessary for sensitivity alone.
n.2: Increased brushing can worsen recession.

Anatomy & Physiology.q: From the image, which structure lies directly beneath enamel?
Anatomy & Physiology.w: Dentine forms the bulk of the tooth and lies directly under enamel.

n.4: The pulp is deeper.
n.1: Cementum is on the root.
n.3: Gingiva is external soft tissue.
n.0: Bone surrounds the tooth, not beneath enamel.

Anatomy & Physiology.q: A dental nurse incorrectly records a lower right canine as 43. What is the correct FDI number?
Anatomy & Physiology.w: The lower right canine is correctly recorded as 43, so there is no error.

n.2: 33 refers to the lower left canine.
n.0: 13 refers to the upper right canine.
n.1: 23 refers to the upper left canine.
n.4: 44 refers to the lower right first premolar.

Anatomy & Physiology.q: During an oral examination, a structure is identified as forming the anterior roof of the mouth and consisting of bone. What is this structure?
Anatomy & Physiology.w: The hard palate forms the anterior bony roof of the oral cavity.

n.2: The soft palate is posterior and not bony.
n.4: The uvula is a soft tissue extension of the soft palate.
n.3: The tongue is located on the floor of the mouth.
n.0: The floor of the mouth is inferior, not part of the roof.

Anatomy & Physiology.q: A dental nurse is asked to confirm the correct sequence of FDI quadrants for permanent teeth. Which is correct?
o: Lower left → Upper left → Lower right → Upper right
Lower right → Lower left → Upper left → Upper right
Upper left → Upper right → Lower right → Lower left
Upper right → Lower right → Upper left → Lower left
Upper right → Upper left → Lower left → Lower right
Anatomy & Physiology.w: The correct FDI quadrant sequence is 1 (upper right), 2 (upper left), 3 (lower left), 4 (lower right).

n.2: This sequence does not follow FDI quadrant numbering.
n.1: FDI starts with upper quadrants, not lower.
n.3: Quadrants are not arranged in this alternating order.
n.0: This does not reflect the standard FDI sequence.

Anatomy & Physiology.q: A child attends with deep pits and fissures on newly erupted first molars. Which action would best reduce plaque accumulation on occlusal surfaces?
Anatomy & Physiology.w: Fissure sealants protect occlusal pits and fissures from plaque accumulation.

n.3: Interdental brushes target proximal surfaces.
n.1: Inner surfaces still require cleaning.
n.2: Brushing once daily is insufficient.
n.4: Mouthwash alone does not remove plaque.

Anatomy & Physiology.q: A chart lists tooth 55 in a child patient. What does this indicate?
Anatomy & Physiology.w: Quadrant 5 represents upper right primary teeth, and tooth 5 is the second molar.

n.2: Upper left primary would be quadrant 6.
n.0: Lower left primary would be quadrant 7.
n.1: Lower right primary would be quadrant 8.
n.3: Permanent teeth use quadrants 1–4, not 5.

Anatomy & Physiology.q: A white spot lesion is noted on a smooth surface during examination. Which structure is most likely to be damaged first in early dental caries?
Anatomy & Physiology.w: Caries begins with demineralisation of enamel.

n.4: Pulp is affected later.
n.1: Dentine is affected after enamel.
n.0: Cementum is not usually first affected.
n.3: The ligament is unrelated to caries.

Anatomy & Physiology.q: A patient has advanced decay reaching the centre of the tooth. What is the best action?
o: Dress the tooth and arrange a routine recall
Place a temporary restoration and review in six months
Take a radiograph and await symptoms
Anatomy & Physiology.w: Decay reaching the pulp typically requires root canal treatment.

n.0: Appropriate for early enamel lesions, not for decay that has reached the pulp.
n.2: A sedative dressing may settle symptoms briefly but leaves an infected pulp untreated.
n.3: Seals the cavity over infected pulp tissue, which will continue to deteriorate.
n.4: A radiograph is useful, but waiting for symptoms delays necessary treatment.

Anatomy & Physiology.q: A nurse is learning to chart restorations on posterior teeth. In what order would you describe the surfaces of a molar moving from the midline outward?
Anatomy & Physiology.w: From the midline outward, the sequence is mesial then distal, with buccal describing outer orientation.

n.1: Distal does not come before mesial from the midline.
n.3: Occlusal is not part of linear positioning.
n.0: Buccal is not part of the midline sequence.
n.4: Occlusal does not relate to midline progression.

Anatomy & Physiology.q: A dental nurse is charting cavities and needs to record the correct surface. Which of the following best describes the mesial surface of a tooth?
Anatomy & Physiology.w: The mesial surface is the surface closest to the midline of the dental arch.

n.2: Surface facing the cheek is buccal.
n.3: Surface facing the tongue is lingual.
n.4: Surface furthest from the midline is distal.
n.0: Chewing surface refers to occlusal.

Anatomy & Physiology.q: A referral letter records treatment carried out on tooth 37. Which of the following best describes the position of tooth 37 in the FDI system?
Anatomy & Physiology.w: Quadrant 3 is lower left and tooth 7 is the second molar.

n.0: Lower left first molar would be 36.
n.3: Lower right second molar would be 47.
n.4: Upper left second molar would be 27.
n.2: Lower right first molar would be 46.

Anatomy & Physiology.q: A dental nurse notes swelling in the inner cheek lining. Which structure is affected?
Anatomy & Physiology.w: The buccal mucosa lines the inner cheeks and is commonly affected by swelling or trauma.

n.2: Labial mucosa lines the inner lips.
n.1: Gingiva surrounds the teeth.
n.3: The soft palate is located at the back of the mouth.
n.4: The tongue is a muscular organ on the floor of the mouth.

Anatomy & Physiology.q: A patient has a swelling in the floor of the mouth that worsens at mealtimes. In what sequence would saliva flow from the submandibular gland to the oral cavity?
Anatomy & Physiology.w: Saliva from the submandibular gland flows through Wharton’s duct into the oral cavity.

n.3: Stensen’s duct is associated with the parotid gland.
n.0: Minor ducts are not the main pathway for submandibular secretion.
n.2: Parotid duct is unrelated to the submandibular gland.
n.1: There is no palatal duct associated with this gland.

Anatomy & Physiology.q: Based on the image, which structure surrounds the root and connects it to bone?
Anatomy & Physiology.w: The periodontal ligament attaches the tooth root to the alveolar bone.

n.0: The bone of the socket itself — the structure the ligament attaches to, not the connector.
n.1: Covers the root and anchors the ligament fibres, but does not span the gap to bone.
n.2: Supports the gingiva above the crest of bone, not within the socket.
n.3: Attaches the gingiva to the tooth surface, not the root to bone.

Anatomy & Physiology.q: A dental nurse is preparing instruments for examination of the floor of the mouth. Which structure is primarily located here?
Anatomy & Physiology.w: The lingual frenulum is a key structure located on the floor of the mouth, attaching the tongue.

n.3: Palatine tonsils are located at the sides of the oropharynx.
n.4: The uvula is part of the soft palate.
n.1: The hard palate forms the roof of the mouth.
n.0: Buccal mucosa lines the inner cheeks.

Anatomy & Physiology.q: A dental nurse notices reduced saliva production from the floor of the mouth during an examination. Which gland should be assessed first?
Anatomy & Physiology.w: The submandibular gland produces a significant portion of saliva and drains into the floor of the mouth.

n.3: The parotid gland drains near the upper molars.
n.1: Labial glands are minor and contribute minimally.
n.0: Buccal glands are minor salivary glands.
n.2: Palatine glands are located in the palate.

Anatomy & Physiology.q: A dental nurse is unsure whether tooth 75 refers to a permanent or primary tooth. What is the best action?
o: Ask the patient which system their previous practice used
Check the quadrant numbering system being used
Record it as a lower left primary molar
Record it as a lower right permanent molar
Use the Palmer notation instead for clarity
Anatomy & Physiology.w: Quadrants 5–8 indicate primary teeth, so confirming the system ensures accurate identification.

n.0: Patients are not expected to know charting notation.
n.2: This is what 75 means in FDI notation, but assuming it without confirming the system risks a charting error.
n.3: Wrong quadrant and wrong dentition under FDI notation.
n.4: Switching systems mid-record makes the notes harder to follow, not clearer.

Anatomy & Physiology.q: A dental nurse is describing the roof of the mouth to a trainee. Which statement correctly describes the posterior part of the palate?
o: It carries the opening of the parotid duct
It is continuous with the floor of the mouth
It is covered by attached gingiva throughout
It is formed by the maxillary and palatine bones
It is muscular and has no bony support
Anatomy & Physiology.w: The soft palate is muscular, whereas the hard palate is bony, so this is an anatomical misidentification.

n.0: The parotid duct opens into the cheek beside the upper molars.
n.1: The palate forms the roof; the floor lies below the tongue.
n.2: Attached gingiva surrounds the teeth, not the palate as a whole.
n.3: That describes the hard palate, which lies anteriorly.

Anatomy & Physiology.q: In the image provided, which structure contains blood vessels and nerves?
Anatomy & Physiology.w: The pulp chamber houses nerves and blood vessels essential for tooth vitality.

n.2: Enamel is non-vital and contains no nerves.
n.1: Dentine transmits stimuli but does not house nerves centrally.
n.0: Cementum is a protective root covering.
n.3: Gingiva is soft tissue around the tooth.

Anatomy & Physiology.q: A chart records a lesion on the distal surface of a canine. Which description matches this location?
Anatomy & Physiology.w: The distal surface is the surface furthest from the midline.

n.2: Surface facing the lips is labial.
n.3: Surface facing the tongue is lingual.
n.1: Closest to the midline is mesial.
n.0: Canines do not have chewing surfaces like molars.

Anatomy & Physiology.q: A dental nurse is reviewing a radiograph showing loss of supporting structures around a tooth. Which structure is primarily responsible for anchoring the tooth within the socket?
Anatomy & Physiology.w: The periodontal ligament attaches the tooth to the alveolar bone, providing support and shock absorption.

n.0: Also lost in periodontal disease, but it is the bone rather than the supporting attachment.
n.1: Covers the root and anchors the fibres rather than forming the support itself.
n.2: Lies above the bone crest and is not the tooth's attachment to bone.
n.3: Seals the gingiva to the tooth surface rather than supporting it.

Anatomy & Physiology.q: A patient bites firmly on a hard sweet and feels the tooth give slightly before returning to position. Which structure is primarily responsible for absorbing occlusal forces during chewing?
Anatomy & Physiology.w: The periodontal ligament acts as a shock absorber during function.

n.0: Receives the load once the ligament has transmitted it.
n.1: Anchors the ligament fibres but has no cushioning role of its own.
n.2: Slightly resilient beneath enamel, but it does not allow the tooth to move within the socket.
n.3: Rigid and resists wear; it does not absorb or redistribute load.

Anatomy & Physiology.q: A patient presents with severe sensitivity to cold after enamel erosion has exposed the underlying tooth layer. Which structure is most likely responsible for transmitting this sensitivity?
Anatomy & Physiology.w: Dentine contains microscopic tubules that transmit stimuli to the pulp, causing sensitivity when exposed.

n.3: Enamel is non-vital and does not transmit sensation.
n.1: Cementum covers the root and is not primarily involved in sensitivity transmission.
n.0: Alveolar bone supports the tooth but does not transmit sensory stimuli.
n.4: Gingiva protects underlying structures but does not transmit sensation.

Anatomy & Physiology.q: A patient presents with gum recession exposing the root surface. Which tissue normally covers the root?
Anatomy & Physiology.w: Cementum covers the root and provides attachment for the periodontal ligament.

n.3: Enamel covers the crown, not the root.
n.2: Dentine lies beneath enamel and cementum.

n.0: The patient should not self-transport in this situation.
n.4: Recovery position is not first-line for a conscious chest pain patient.

Medical Emergencies.q: During treatment, a patient suddenly becomes pale, sweaty and says they feel faint after seeing the local anaesthetic needle. What is the most likely emergency being recognised?
Medical Emergencies.w: Pallor, sweating and feeling faint triggered by anxiety are classic features of vasovagal syncope.

n.0: Asthma usually presents with wheeze, breathlessness and chest tightness.
n.2: Seizure would more commonly involve altered consciousness or convulsive activity.
n.3: Hyperglycaemia develops more gradually and commonly causes thirst or lethargy.
n.1: Anaphylaxis often includes airway, breathing or skin changes after exposure.

Medical Emergencies.q: A patient is not breathing normally and rescue breaths are required. Which item is most appropriate basic equipment to assist ventilation during a medical emergency?
Medical Emergencies.w: A pocket mask is designed to help deliver rescue breaths more safely during resuscitation.

n.2: An impression tray is not used for ventilation.
n.0: A cheek retractor does not provide assisted ventilation.
n.1: An endodontic ruler is unrelated to airway support.
n.4: A wax knife has no emergency airway function.

Medical Emergencies.q: An AED advises a shock. What is the best action immediately before pressing the shock button?
o: Ensure nobody is touching the patient
Remove both pads and dry the chest again
Medical Emergencies.w: Before shock delivery, everyone must be clear of contact with the patient for safety and effective shock administration.

n.2: Do not delay a prompted shock to give breaths.
n.4: If a shock is advised, it should be delivered promptly.
n.3: Pads should remain in place unless incorrectly attached.
n.0: A prolonged pulse check delays defibrillation.

Medical Emergencies.q: The AED announces, 'No shock advised.' The patient remains unresponsive and not breathing normally. What is the best action?
o: Place the patient in the recovery position and monitor
Remove the pads since no shock is required
Repeat the analysis immediately to confirm the reading
Resume CPR immediately until the AED re-analyses or the patient recovers
Switch to rescue breaths alone until help arrives
Medical Emergencies.w: If no shock is advised and the patient remains in cardiac arrest, CPR should continue immediately.

n.0: The recovery position is for someone breathing normally, which this patient is not.
n.1: The rhythm may become shockable; the pads stay on.
n.2: Re-analysing straight away delays compressions for no benefit.
n.4: Ventilation without compressions provides no circulation.

Medical Emergencies.q: During AED analysis, a team member continues chest compressions. How should this be interpreted?
o: This improves accuracy by keeping circulation moving
This is acceptable if compressions are shallow
This is required whenever only one rescuer is present
This may interfere with rhythm analysis and should stop when prompted
This prevents the AED from advising an unnecessary shock
Medical Emergencies.w: Movement during analysis can interfere with rhythm detection, so compressions should stop when the AED instructs.

n.0: Although compressions are important, they should pause briefly for analysis when prompted.
n.2: Single-rescuer CPR still follows AED voice prompts.
n.4: Continuing movement can reduce analysis accuracy, not improve it.
n.1: Compression depth is unrelated to the need to pause for analysis.

Medical Emergencies.q: A diabetic patient becomes shaky, confused and sweaty while waiting for treatment after missing lunch. What is the most likely emergency?
Medical Emergencies.w: Sweating, tremor and confusion in a diabetic who has missed food strongly suggest hypoglycaemia.

n.1: Hyperventilation causes rapid breathing and tingling rather than low glucose symptoms.
n.0: Hyperglycaemia is typically slower in onset and less associated with sweating.
n.4: TIA causes focal neurological symptoms rather than typical low glucose signs.
n.3: MI may cause chest pain or collapse rather than classic low glucose presentation.

Medical Emergencies.q: CPR is in progress and the AED has analysed the rhythm. The AED says, 'Shock advised.' What is the most appropriate action immediately before pressing the shock button?
o: Check for signs of circulation for 30 seconds
Continue compressions while the shock is delivered
Ensure everyone is clear and nobody is touching the patient
Give two rescue breaths to improve oxygenation first
Remove one pad briefly and reapply it
Medical Emergencies.w: Before shock delivery, all rescuers must be clear of the patient to avoid harm and allow safe defibrillation.

n.3: Breaths should not delay a shock once advised.
n.0: A prolonged circulation check delays defibrillation.
n.4: Pads should stay attached unless incorrectly placed.
n.1: No one should touch the patient during shock delivery.

Medical Emergencies.q: A patient develops wheeze and increasing breathlessness during treatment. They have their reliever inhaler with them. What is the best immediate management?
o: Give two puffs of their preventer inhaler and continue
Help the patient use their reliever inhaler and sit upright
Lay the patient flat and give the reliever inhaler
Reassure the patient and delay the inhaler until the wheeze worsens
Use the reliever inhaler only if oxygen has been given first
Medical Emergencies.w: For an asthma attack, assist with reliever inhaler use and position comfortably upright.

n.0: A preventer works over weeks and does nothing in an acute attack.
n.2: Lying flat worsens breathlessness; the patient should sit up.
n.3: Treatment should not wait for deterioration.
n.4: The reliever comes first and does not depend on oxygen.

Medical Emergencies.q: A patient is found slumped in the waiting room and does not respond when spoken to. Which finding most strongly identifies that CPR should be started immediately on an adult patient?
o: Drowsy with a weak radial pulse
Medical Emergencies.w: CPR is indicated when the patient is unresponsive and not breathing normally after assessment.

n.3: This may indicate illness but does not by itself indicate cardiac arrest.
n.0: The patient is breathing and requires urgent assessment, not immediate CPR.
n.2: Presence of circulation signs means cardiac arrest is not confirmed.
n.1: This suggests possible postural hypotension or other causes, not arrest.

Medical Emergencies.q: A patient has chest pain, becomes grey, clammy and increasingly short of breath. Which sequence of recognition priorities is best?
o: Recognise mild indigestion then continue treatment
Recognise possible acute coronary syndrome and worsening circulation
Medical Emergencies.w: Chest pain with pallor, clamminess and breathlessness suggests serious cardiac compromise.

n.0: Serious causes must be considered first, not indigestion.
n.1: Needle phobia does not explain progressive chest symptoms.
n.4: Muscle strain is less likely with systemic deterioration.
n.3: Postural dizziness does not fit persistent chest pain and breathlessness.

Medical Emergencies.q: While attaching AED pads, a colleague places one pad directly over a visible medication patch on the chest. What should be done?
o: Delay pad placement until the patient regains consciousness
Leave the patch in place because it improves adhesion
Place the second pad over the same patch for balance
Remove or avoid the patch area and place the pad on clean dry skin
Use only one pad if a patch is present
Medical Emergencies.w: Pads should not be placed over medication patches. The patch should be removed or avoided according to training, then pads applied to dry skin.

n.1: Patches may interfere with contact and create risk.
n.2: Both pads should not be placed over the same area.
n.0: Defibrillation should not be delayed unnecessarily.
n.4: AEDs require two pads unless device-specific instructions state otherwise.

Medical Emergencies.q: A patient collapses in the surgery. After confirming unresponsiveness and calling for help, what sequence should follow?
o: Check blood pressure, give oxygen, then assess airway
Give rescue breaths first, then check responsiveness
Move patient to wheelchair, then assess breathing
Open airway, assess breathing, start compressions if not breathing normally
Medical Emergencies.w: After calling for help, airway and breathing are assessed promptly; if breathing is absent or abnormal, CPR begins.

n.1: Blood pressure measurement delays life-saving assessment.
n.3: Moving the patient unnecessarily delays treatment.
n.0: Breathing assessment should not be skipped.
n.2: Responsiveness is checked before deciding on CPR.

Medical Emergencies.q: A patient is lying on a wet floor after collapse. CPR is in progress and the AED is ready. What is the best action?
o: Continue compressions in the water and shock as normal
Dry the chest only and shock without moving the patient
Move or dry the patient away from pooled water before shock delivery if it can be done quickly
Postpone defibrillation and continue compressions only
Use half the usual energy setting to allow for the water
Medical Emergencies.w: Water presents a hazard. The patient should be moved or the area dried promptly if feasible, while maintaining resuscitation efforts.

n.0: Pooled water can conduct current to rescuers.
n.1: Drying the chest is essential and may be enough, but standing water around the patient still poses a risk.
n.3: Compressions alone will not correct a shockable rhythm.
n.4: AED energy is fixed and cannot be adjusted for conditions.

Medical Emergencies.q: A conscious diabetic patient becomes sweaty, shaky and confused. Which basic emergency item is most appropriate to prepare first?
Medical Emergencies.w: Likely hypoglycaemia in a conscious patient is commonly managed initially with a fast-acting glucose source if safe to swallow.

n.4: Rubber dam equipment is unrelated to low blood glucose treatment.
n.2: A matrix band is restorative equipment, not emergency equipment.
n.0: Etching gel is not used in medical emergencies.
n.3: A mouth mirror has no therapeutic role here.

Medical Emergencies.q: A patient becomes unresponsive with tonic-clonic limb movements and jaw clenching. What emergency is most likely being recognised?
Medical Emergencies.w: Loss of consciousness with tonic-clonic movements is typical of a generalised seizure.

n.0: Rapid onset with skin, airway and circulatory signs rather than tonic-clonic movement.
n.2: Can progress to fitting, but is usually preceded by confusion, sweating and hunger.
n.3: Typically causes focal weakness or speech disturbance rather than generalised convulsion.
n.4: The closest mimic — brief jerking can follow a faint, but it settles quickly on lying flat.

Medical Emergencies.q: A patient develops facial swelling, wheeze and feels faint after exposure to latex. What is the best action?
o: Ask the patient to walk outside for air
Continue treatment because symptoms may settle
Offer water and observe for ten minutes
Treat as anaphylaxis and administer adrenaline if trained and available
Medical Emergencies.w: Airway, breathing and circulatory symptoms after exposure suggest anaphylaxis requiring urgent treatment.

n.3: Observation alone is unsafe in suspected anaphylaxis.
n.0: Walking may worsen collapse risk.
n.1: Dental treatment must stop during an emergency.
n.2: GTN does not treat allergic reactions.

Medical Emergencies.q: A patient collapses and is unresponsive with abnormal breathing. Which equipment should be brought immediately if available?
Medical Emergencies.w: For suspected cardiac arrest, an AED should be retrieved urgently alongside CPR measures.

n.1: Needed, but defibrillation is the time-critical intervention.
n.2: Useful for airway management rather than the immediate priority.
n.3: Monitoring equipment; it does not treat the arrest.
n.4: Supports ventilation but does not address a shockable rhythm.

Medical Emergencies.q: A patient with stroke symptoms is conscious and breathing normally. Which management approach is most appropriate?
o: Ask them to walk to the car for hospital transfer
Call emergency services promptly and monitor airway and responsiveness
Give them oral glucose routinely before assessment
Lay them fully flat and leave them alone
Medical Emergencies.w: Suspected stroke requires urgent emergency referral with close monitoring.

n.3: Glucose is not routinely given without indication.
n.4: Leaving the patient unattended is unsafe.
n.2: Treatment should cease immediately.
n.0: The patient should not self-mobilise or self-transport.

Medical Emergencies.q: A patient recovers after a fainting episode. Which sequence is most appropriate before discharge?
o: Allow them to leave once colour has returned
Give oral glucose, then discharge once they can stand
Reassess fully, allow gradual sitting up, confirm recovery, then decide on discharge
Return them to an upright position and resume treatment
Sit them up immediately and observe for five minutes
Medical Emergencies.w: Patients recovering from syncope should be reassessed and returned upright gradually once stable.

n.0: Colour alone is not evidence of full recovery.
n.1: Glucose treats hypoglycaemia, which is a different cause.
n.3: Resuming before full recovery risks a further episode.
n.4: Sitting up too quickly commonly causes a second faint.

Medical Emergencies.q: A patient with a history of angina develops central chest pressure during treatment that improves after using their GTN spray. Which condition is most likely recognised?
Medical Emergencies.w: Chest discomfort relieved by GTN in a patient with known angina is consistent with an angina episode.

n.0: Possible, but it would not typically be relieved by glyceryl trinitrate.
n.1: Can mimic cardiac pain, though it does not respond to GTN.
n.3: The key distinction: pain at rest, worsening, or not relieved by GTN. Here it settled with the spray.
n.4: Would involve pallor, sweating and a falling blood pressure.

Medical Emergencies.q: A patient is breathing rapidly, has tingling fingers, dizziness and appears very anxious after treatment starts. What is the most likely emergency being recognised?
Medical Emergencies.w: Rapid breathing with tingling and anxiety is consistent with hyperventilation.

n.4: Stroke more commonly causes focal neurological deficits.
n.3: Hypoglycaemia commonly causes sweating and confusion rather than tingling from overbreathing.
n.1: Anaphylaxis usually involves allergic signs such as rash or wheeze.
n.0: Airway obstruction would impair airflow rather than cause overbreathing.

Medical Emergencies.q: A conscious diabetic patient is shaky, confused and sweating. They are able to swallow safely. What is the best action?
o: Give fast-acting glucose and reassess response
Give GTN spray under the tongue
Place them in the recovery position immediately
Withhold all oral intake and continue observing
Medical Emergencies.w: A conscious patient with likely hypoglycaemia who can swallow should receive fast-acting glucose promptly.

n.2: Recovery position is for an unconscious breathing patient.
n.1: GTN is used for angina, not low blood glucose.
n.4: Delaying treatment may worsen hypoglycaemia.
n.3: CPR is not indicated in a conscious responsive patient.

Medical Emergencies.q: A patient is hyperventilating, anxious and tingling in the fingers but remains responsive. What is the best immediate action?
o: Force the patient to breathe into a paper bag
Place the patient prone on the floor
Reassure, stop treatment and coach slow controlled breathing
Medical Emergencies.w: Supportive reassurance and slowing breathing are appropriate for hyperventilation once serious causes are excluded.

n.1: Adrenaline is not indicated for simple hyperventilation.
n.2: Prone positioning is unnecessary and unhelpful.
n.4: CPR is not indicated in a responsive patient.
n.0: Paper bag breathing is not recommended.

Medical Emergencies.q: A patient treated for hypoglycaemia becomes alert and symptoms resolve. What is the best next step?
o: Give GTN spray to prevent relapse
Lay the patient flat for one hour regardless of condition
Monitor, provide longer-acting carbohydrate if appropriate, and reassess
Send the patient home alone at once
Medical Emergencies.w: After recovery, continued monitoring and follow-up carbohydrate intake may help maintain glucose levels.

n.3: Immediate treatment restart may be inappropriate.
n.4: Abrupt discharge without reassessment may be unsafe.
n.0: GTN has no role in hypoglycaemia management.
n.1: Positioning should reflect the patient's condition, not a fixed rule.

Medical Emergencies.q: During CPR, chest compressions are being delivered too slowly at around 60 per minute. Which interpretation is most accurate?
o: The rate is acceptable when two rescuers are present
The rate is ideal if compressions are deeper
The rate is inadequate and should be increased
The rate only matters once the AED arrives
The rate should be reduced further to avoid fatigue
Medical Emergencies.w: An adult compression rate of about 100–120 per minute is recommended, so 60 per minute is too slow.

n.1: Depth does not compensate for an inadequate compression rate.
n.0: Two rescuers do not change the target compression rate.
n.4: Reducing the rate further would worsen perfusion.
n.3: Effective compressions matter immediately, not only after AED arrival.

Medical Emergencies.q: A patient begins to struggle for breath partway through a meal in the waiting area. Which feature best identifies airway obstruction in a conscious adult patient?
o: Unable to speak or cough effectively
Warm flushed skin with no distress
Medical Emergencies.w: Inability to speak or cough effectively suggests severe airway obstruction.

n.0: Toothache alone does not indicate choking.
n.4: No distress signs make airway obstruction unlikely.
n.2: Speaking normally suggests airway patency.
n.1: Headache alone does not indicate obstruction.

Medical Emergencies.q: An adult in cardiac arrest has just been defibrillated. After a shock is delivered, what sequence should follow next?
o: Check for a pulse and breathing before continuing
Remove the pads and reassess the airway
Resume CPR immediately and follow further AED prompts
Wait for the AED to confirm the rhythm has changed
Watch for signs of life for thirty seconds before restarting
Medical Emergencies.w: CPR should restart immediately after a shock unless the patient shows clear signs of recovery, following AED prompts.

n.0: A return of circulation is uncommon immediately after a shock, and checking wastes compression time.
n.1: Pads stay on so the AED can re-analyse.
n.3: The AED will re-analyse after two minutes; compressions continue meanwhile.
n.4: Half a minute without compressions after a shock is a significant loss.

Medical Emergencies.q: A practice is reviewing its medical emergency preparedness after a near miss. Which shortcoming regarding emergency drugs and equipment is most serious?
o: Not knowing where the emergency kit is stored
Training staff to locate the AED
Medical Emergencies.w: If staff cannot locate the emergency kit quickly, critical treatment may be dangerously delayed.

n.0: Routine expiry checks are good practice.
n.3: Replacing used stock is appropriate and necessary.
n.1: Checklists support readiness rather than create risk.
n.4: Training staff to find the AED improves emergency response.

Medical Emergencies.q: A patient becomes unresponsive in the waiting area, is not breathing normally, and no pulse is detected. What is the most appropriate immediate action?
o: Begin chest compressions and call for the AED
Check the pulse again for a full minute
Give high-flow oxygen and observe for response
Move the patient to the dental chair before acting
Place the patient in the recovery position
Medical Emergencies.w: When a patient is unresponsive, not breathing normally and has no pulse, CPR should start immediately while another team member retrieves the AED.

n.4: Recovery position is only appropriate for a breathing unconscious patient.
n.2: Oxygen may be helpful later, but delaying compressions reduces survival chances.
n.1: Pulse checks should be brief; prolonged reassessment delays CPR.
n.3: Moving the patient first wastes critical time unless the environment is unsafe.

Medical Emergencies.q: A colleague calls for help because a patient has collapsed in the waiting room. Which item is most important to bring first when responding to a collapsed patient elsewhere in the practice?
o: Emergency drugs kit and AED if available
Medical Emergencies.w: Emergency response equipment such as the AED and emergency kit should be prioritised.

n.0: Administrative items are not immediate priorities.
n.3: Routine dental instruments are not first-line emergency equipment.
n.4: These may help later but are not priorities.
n.2: Impression materials are unrelated.

Medical Emergencies.q: During CPR, the chest is not returning fully to its normal position between compressions. What should be corrected?
o: Compressing at too shallow a depth between breaths
Compressing the chest at too fast a rate
Interrupting compressions to check the pulse
Leaning on the chest between compressions
Pausing compressions for too long during rescue breaths
Medical Emergencies.w: Leaning prevents full chest recoil, reducing venous return and CPR effectiveness.

n.0: A real fault, but the description is of incomplete recoil rather than depth.
n.1: Also a common error, but rate is not what stops the chest recoiling.
n.2: Reduces compression fraction; it does not prevent recoil.
n.4: Another genuine fault, but again not the one described.

Medical Emergencies.q: In a crowded waiting room, the AED has advised a shock. Which scenario-based action is best?
o: Ask one person to hold the patient still while shocking
Delay indefinitely until the waiting room is empty
Loudly instruct everyone to stand clear, visually confirm, then deliver the shock
Press shock immediately because voice prompts are enough warning
Remove the pads to make space around the patient
Medical Emergencies.w: The rescuer should clearly warn others, visually confirm nobody is touching the patient, then deliver the shock promptly.

n.3: Visual confirmation is still required.
n.0: Nobody should be touching the patient during shock delivery.
n.4: Pads should remain attached for defibrillation.
n.1: Unnecessary delay reduces the chance of successful defibrillation.

Medical Emergencies.q: During treatment, a patient says their tongue feels swollen and their voice sounds hoarse shortly after taking medication. What is the best recognition?
o: Local anaesthetic toxicity affecting the airway
Normal numbness following an inferior dental block
Possible evolving anaphylaxis with airway involvement
Soft tissue swelling from the injection itself
Medical Emergencies.w: Tongue swelling and hoarse voice may indicate airway oedema in anaphylaxis.

n.0: Toxicity causes tinnitus, metallic taste and restlessness rather than airway swelling.
n.1: Numbness does not make the voice hoarse.
n.3: Would be localised and would not affect the voice.
n.4: Causes pallor and faintness, not tongue swelling.

Medical Emergencies.q: A patient in the waiting room is clutching their throat and their cough has become weak and silent. Which action best identifies correct management of a conscious choking patient with ineffective cough?
o: Encourage them to keep coughing and monitor closely
Give five back blows followed by five abdominal thrusts
Lay the patient flat and begin chest compressions
Perform a finger sweep of the mouth to find the obstruction
Sit the patient upright and offer sips of water
Medical Emergencies.w: An ineffective cough in a conscious patient suggests severe choking requiring prompt intervention.

n.0: Correct for mild choking with an effective cough — but this cough is ineffective.
n.2: Compressions are for a patient who has become unresponsive.
n.3: Blind finger sweeps can push the obstruction further down.
n.4: Fluid cannot clear an obstructed airway and risks worsening it.

Medical Emergencies.q: A conscious patient is clutching their throat, unable to speak and making silent efforts to breathe. What should be recognised first?
o: Mild choking with an effective cough
Medical Emergencies.w: Inability to speak with silent respiratory effort suggests severe choking.

n.0: Produces wheeze and difficulty breathing, but the patient can usually still speak.
n.1: Genuinely mimics this, but would normally follow an allergen and show skin or circulatory signs.
n.2: The key distinction: in mild choking the patient can cough forcefully and often speak. Silence means the obstruction is severe.
n.4: Causes pallor and collapse, not a clutched throat with silent breathing efforts.

Medical Emergencies.q: After local anaesthetic, a patient reports ringing in the ears, metallic taste and becomes restless. Which emergency may need recognising?
o: An allergic reaction to the local anaesthetic
Simple anxiety following the local anaesthetic injection
Vasovagal syncope after the local anaesthetic
Medical Emergencies.w: Tinnitus, metallic taste and agitation after injection may indicate local anaesthetic toxicity.

n.0: The important distinction: allergy causes rash, swelling and airway or circulatory signs, not tinnitus and metallic taste.
n.1: A cause of toxicity rather than the recognition itself.
n.3: Anxiety does not produce a metallic taste or ringing in the ears.
n.4: Would cause pallor, sweating and a slow pulse.

Medical Emergencies.q: During two-person CPR in the practice, compressions are effective but ventilation attempts are repeatedly failing because the chest is not rising. What scenario-based response is most appropriate?
o: Continue ineffective breaths without changing technique
Move the patient onto the dental chair immediately
Remove the AED pads to improve access
Reopen the airway and attempt a better seal before the next breaths
Stop compressions until perfect ventilations are achieved
Medical Emergencies.w: If the chest is not rising, airway position and mask seal should be corrected while minimising interruptions to compressions.

n.4: Compressions should continue with only brief pauses as needed.
n.2: AED pads should remain attached once applied.
n.0: Persisting with ineffective technique does not oxygenate the patient.
n.1: Unnecessary movement delays ongoing resuscitation.

Medical Emergencies.q: An adult patient is in cardiac arrest and the AED pads are being opened. Which option correctly identifies the usual adult AED pad placement?
o: Both pads on the lower left chest wall together
Both pads placed centrally over the sternum
One pad on each shoulder only
One pad on the abdomen and one on the sternum
One pad upper right chest, one pad left side below the armpit
Medical Emergencies.w: Standard adult pad placement is upper right chest and left lateral chest below the armpit unless pads indicate otherwise.

n.1: Pads should be separated to allow current to pass through the heart.
n.2: Shoulders are not standard defibrillation pad sites.
n.0: Pads placed together on one side are ineffective.
n.3: Abdominal placement is not standard for AED use.

Medical Emergencies.q: A team is running a simulated cardiac arrest as part of annual training. Which failing during CPR is most serious?
o: Stopping compressions for long unnecessary pauses
Medical Emergencies.w: Long interruptions reduce circulation and worsen CPR effectiveness.

n.1: Counting aloud may improve coordination.
n.3: Changing rescuers can maintain quality compressions.
n.4: AED use is beneficial.
n.0: Early escalation is appropriate.

Medical Emergencies.q: A patient with known epilepsy begins convulsing in the dental chair. During a seizure, which action is most appropriate?
o: Hold the limbs firmly to stop jerking
Insert a mouth prop between the teeth
Move the patient immediately to another room
Protect the patient from injury and do not restrain movements
Medical Emergencies.w: The priority during seizure activity is preventing injury while allowing the seizure to run its course.

n.2: Nothing should be placed in the mouth during a seizure.
n.1: Restraint can cause injury.
n.0: Oral fluids are unsafe during a seizure.
n.3: Moving the patient may increase injury risk.

Medical Emergencies.q: A collapsed patient makes occasional noisy, irregular efforts to draw air. Which misinterpretation is most concerning when assessing a collapsed patient?
o: Asking for the patient’s medical history
Checking whether the area is safe
Mistaking agonal gasps for normal breathing
Moving instruments away from the chair
Medical Emergencies.w: Agonal gasps can occur in cardiac arrest and must not be mistaken for normal breathing.

n.0: History may be useful if time and condition allow, but is not the key recognition error here.
n.4: Making the area safer is appropriate.
n.1: Calling for help early is good practice.
n.2: Scene safety assessment is appropriate.

Medical Emergencies.q: A colleague is performing CPR and asks you to take over compressions because they are tiring. What is the best action?
o: Complete the current cycle of thirty compressions, then swap
Swap at the next rhythm check to avoid interrupting compressions
Swap compressors quickly with minimal interruption
Swap once the airway adjunct has been fitted
Take over only when the tiring rescuer stops on their own
Medical Emergencies.w: Compressors should be changed promptly with minimal pause to maintain compression quality.

n.0: Reasonable, but a tiring rescuer's compressions are already losing depth.
n.1: The ideal moment when it is close, but waiting several minutes while quality falls is worse than a two-second swap.
n.3: Ties compressor change to an unrelated task.
n.4: By then compression quality has usually fallen well below what is effective.

Medical Emergencies.q: A patient arrests in a cramped decontamination room. The floor is safe but space is limited. Which scenario-based decision is best?
o: Move the patient only far enough to kneel beside the chest
Move the patient to the recovery area before starting compressions
Reposition the furniture first, then start compressions
Start compressions from the head end because of the limited space
Start CPR where the patient is and relocate only if essential
Medical Emergencies.w: If the area is safe, CPR should begin immediately. Relocation should only occur if absolutely necessary.

n.0: Tempting, and sometimes necessary — but it still delays the first compressions.
n.1: Any move delays compressions, and time without them costs survival.
n.2: Clearing space matters, but not before compressions have begun.
n.3: Compressions from the head cannot be delivered effectively or safely.

Medical Emergencies.q: A patient has a prominent pacemaker bulge below the right clavicle. How should AED pad placement be managed?
o: Avoid using the AED because pacemakers prevent shocks
Delay defibrillation until the device type is confirmed
Place the pad away from the device, not directly over it
Place the pad directly on the pacemaker for best contact
Use only posterior pad placement and no chest pads
Medical Emergencies.w: Pads should not be placed directly over an implanted device; they should be positioned nearby according to guidance.

n.3: Direct placement over the device is not recommended.
n.0: AEDs can still be used on patients with pacemakers.
n.4: Routine AED use does not require abandoning standard pad placement unless necessary.
n.1: Treatment should not be delayed for device identification.

Medical Emergencies.q: A patient who has just received latex exposure develops wheeze, lip swelling, widespread rash and feels faint. What is the most likely emergency?
Medical Emergencies.w: Airway swelling, wheeze, rash and circulatory compromise after exposure indicate anaphylaxis.

n.3: Simple urticaria does not usually include airway or circulatory compromise.
n.1: Angina causes chest discomfort rather than allergic features.
n.2: Hypoglycaemia does not cause lip swelling or rash.
n.4: Syncope does not explain wheeze and allergic swelling.

Medical Emergencies.q: A patient with asthma cannot complete sentences, is wheezing and using accessory muscles to breathe. Which interpretation is most accurate?
o: This is a mild asthma exacerbation that will settle with reassurance
This is an expected response to local anaesthetic
This is anxiety-related hyperventilation rather than asthma
This suggests a severe asthma attack requiring urgent escalation
This suggests upper airway obstruction rather than asthma
Medical Emergencies.w: Inability to complete sentences with wheeze and increased effort indicates severe respiratory compromise.

n.0: The closest wrong answer — but inability to complete sentences and accessory muscle use mark this as severe.
n.1: Not a recognised effect of local anaesthetic.
n.2: Hyperventilation does not usually produce wheeze or accessory muscle use.
n.4: Obstruction gives stridor rather than expiratory wheeze.

Medical Emergencies.q: A patient complains of crushing central chest pain radiating to the jaw and feels nauseated. GTN has not relieved symptoms. What should be recognised?
Medical Emergencies.w: Persistent crushing chest pain radiating to jaw with nausea may indicate myocardial infarction.

n.4: Indigestion can mimic pain but serious cardiac causes must be recognised.
n.0: Hyperventilation usually presents with rapid breathing and tingling.

n.1: Polishing paste shade is unrelated to oral surgery.
n.0: Impression trays are not the first priority.

Clinical Procedures.q: The operator asks for composite to be placed in several small increments rather than one large bulk. What is the most likely interpretation?
o: Incremental placement is being used to improve curing and limit shrinkage stress
The aim is to reduce the number of instruments required chairside
The cavity preparation is unsuitable for bonding agents
The operator wants the final restoration to appear more translucent
This method is mainly to avoid the need for any finishing or polishing
Clinical Procedures.w: Composite is often placed incrementally to improve depth of cure and reduce polymerisation shrinkage stress within the restoration.

n.3: Appearance can be influenced by layering, but the primary reason here is material performance rather than translucency alone.
n.2: Incremental placement does not indicate that bonding agents are unsuitable.
n.4: Finishing and polishing may still be required after incremental placement.
n.1: Instrument count is not the main reason for choosing an incremental technique.

Clinical Procedures.q: The nurse notices the curing light tip is heavily covered with composite residue. What is the most likely consequence if it is used unchanged?
o: Reduced light output reaching the restoration
Clinical Procedures.w: Residue on the tip can block transmitted light and reduce curing effectiveness.

n.0: Etching is unrelated to curing light contamination.
n.2: Matrix fracture is not caused by the light tip.
n.3: Amalgam trituration is unrelated.
n.1: Glass ionomer setting chemistry is unrelated.

Clinical Procedures.q: While assisting with placement of a matrix band for a Class II restoration, the patient closes suddenly with instruments in place. What is the best action?
o: Ask the patient to remain still and continue immediately
Place the restorative material without further delay
Tighten the matrix band quickly before the patient moves again
Use suction to improve visibility and continue the procedure
Withdraw instruments safely and check for injury before proceeding
Clinical Procedures.w: The priority is to withdraw instruments safely and assess whether any injury has occurred before treatment continues.

n.0: Continuing immediately without checking safety increases the risk of trauma.
n.2: Attempting to complete a step quickly in an unsafe moment could worsen injury.
n.3: Improved visibility does not address the immediate need to protect the patient.
n.1: Material placement should not continue until safety has been restored and any trauma assessed.

Clinical Procedures.q: A mixing pad has been contaminated by spray before glass ionomer is prepared. What is the best action?
o: Replace the pad and prepare a clean mixing surface
Use only material from the centre of the pad
Use the damp area because liquid is already present
Clinical Procedures.w: Contamination alters proportions and handling. A clean, dry mixing surface should be used.

n.4: Unknown moisture content can compromise the mix.
n.0: Changing powder ratio is inaccurate.
n.1: Speed does not correct contamination.
n.3: The whole pad may be affected.

Clinical Procedures.q: A patient is having a chipped incisor repaired with composite. Which material is commonly used to etch enamel before placing a bonded composite restoration?
Clinical Procedures.w: Phosphoric acid gel is routinely used for enamel etching before bonding.

n.1: Eugenol paste is not an etchant.

n.4: Zinc phosphate is a cement, not an etchant.

Clinical Procedures.q: During root surface debridement, visibility becomes poor due to mist. What is the best action by the nurse?
Clinical Procedures.w: Correct suction positioning helps control spray and improve visibility.

n.2: Reducing lighting worsens visibility.
n.1: Shade guides are unrelated.
n.0: Records are not the priority during active treatment.
n.3: Removing the bib clip does not manage mist.

Clinical Procedures.q: Paper points inserted after irrigation are still emerging noticeably wet. What is the most likely interpretation?
o: The access cavity outline is ideal
The canal has definitely been over-instrumented
The canal may not yet be dry enough for obturation
The master cone fit has been confirmed
The temporary restoration can now be placed
Clinical Procedures.w: Persistently wet paper points suggest that the canal may still contain moisture and may not yet be ready for obturation.

n.3: Paper point wetness does not confirm the fit of the master cone.
n.0: Access cavity design is not determined by whether paper points emerge wet.
n.1: Moist paper points alone do not prove over-instrumentation.
n.4: Moisture control within the canal is a separate issue from placing a temporary restoration.

Clinical Procedures.q: During etching for an anterior composite restoration, the nurse notices saliva contamination on the prepared tooth before bonding. What is the best action?
o: Apply additional etchant without informing the operator
Dry the area forcefully for longer and continue without mentioning it
Inform the operator immediately so the surface can be managed appropriately
Place the first composite increment quickly before more moisture appears
Proceed with bonding to avoid overdrying the tooth
Clinical Procedures.w: Saliva contamination can compromise bonding, so the operator should be informed immediately so the surface can be re-managed appropriately.

n.4: Proceeding without correcting contamination risks reduced bond effectiveness and restoration failure.
n.1: Forceful drying alone does not reliably correct contamination and may introduce further problems.
n.3: Composite should not be placed onto a surface that may be compromised.
n.0: Re-etching may or may not be required, but it should not be done unilaterally without informing the operator.

Clinical Procedures.q: Paper points placed in a canal are repeatedly coming out heavily wet after irrigation. What is the most likely interpretation?
o: The access cavity is too small for instrumentation
The canal may not yet be sufficiently dried for obturation
The file sequence has been completed incorrectly
The master cone fit is already confirmed
Working length has definitely been lost
Clinical Procedures.w: Persistently wet paper points suggest the canal is not yet sufficiently dry, which may mean obturation should not proceed at that stage.

n.3: Moisture on paper points does not confirm master cone fit.
n.4: Wet paper points alone do not prove that working length has been lost.
n.0: Access size may affect handling, but repeated wetness mainly indicates moisture within the canal.
n.2: File sequence issues are not the most direct interpretation of persistently wet paper points.

Clinical Procedures.q: A temporary crown cement dislodges soon after seating and appears watery. What is the most likely interpretation?
o: The crown margin was polished too much
The mix ratio may have been incorrect
Clinical Procedures.w: A thin watery mix may reduce retention and indicate incorrect powder-liquid proportioning.

n.2: Ideal occlusion does not explain weak cement.
n.0: Polishing margins is not the likely cause.
n.4: Isolation does not make cement watery.
n.3: Shade is irrelevant to retention.

Clinical Procedures.q: After placement of a temporary dressing, the patient says the tooth feels high on biting. What is the best action?
o: Advise the patient that a new dressing always feels high at first
Advise the patient to eat on the other side until it settles
Ask the operator to check occlusion before dismissal
Book a review appointment for the following week
Reassure the patient and ask them to call if it persists
Clinical Procedures.w: A high restoration should be assessed and adjusted by the operator before the patient leaves.

n.0: A high dressing can cause pain and fracture; it should not be normalised.
n.1: Manages the symptom while leaving the occlusion uncorrected.
n.3: A week of traumatic occlusion when it can be checked now.
n.4: Puts the responsibility on the patient for something checkable immediately.

Clinical Procedures.q: Two days after a deep posterior restoration, the patient reports sensitivity on biting. Which interpretation is most appropriate to relay to the operator?
o: The complaint proves the local anaesthetic has not fully worn off
The patient should simply avoid chewing on that side for several months
The restoration may need review for occlusion, pulpal response or marginal seal
The symptoms confirm that extraction is now required
This finding means the matrix band used was too wide
Clinical Procedures.w: Post-operative biting sensitivity can have several causes, including high occlusion, pulpal irritation or marginal issues, so a clinical review is appropriate.

n.3: Sensitivity alone does not confirm that extraction is necessary.
n.0: Two days later, persistent biting sensitivity is unlikely to be explained solely by residual anaesthetic.
n.4: Matrix width alone does not adequately explain the range of causes for post-operative biting sensitivity.
n.1: Avoidance without review risks missing a problem that may need correction.

Clinical Procedures.q: Using the image, identify item number 5.

n.4: Elevators have heavier working ends.
n.0: Bracket pliers are orthodontic instruments.
n.3: Needle holders have locking handles.
n.2: Crown forceps are shaped differently for grasping crowns.

Clinical Procedures.q: A deep occlusal cavity in a lower molar is being restored with amalgam. Which instrument is specifically designed to compact amalgam into a cavity preparation during placement?
Clinical Procedures.w: A condenser is used to compact amalgam into the cavity, helping reduce voids and improve adaptation.

n.0: A burnisher is used more for smoothing and contouring rather than condensing amalgam into place.
n.2: An excavator is mainly used to remove soft carious tissue or debris.
n.3: A plastic instrument is commonly used for handling restorative materials such as composite, not condensing amalgam.
n.4: A scaler is used for periodontal instrumentation rather than restorative condensation.

Clinical Procedures.q: A file is dropped onto a non-sterile surface during preparation of the second canal. What is the best action?
o: Put it aside and use it later if needed
Replace it with a sterile file of the same size and type
Return it to use if it has not visibly soiled
Rinse it in irrigant and continue
Wipe it with alcohol and use it for the coronal third only
Clinical Procedures.w: Once contaminated, the file should be replaced with a sterile equivalent to maintain asepsis during treatment.

n.3: Irrigant is not a substitute for sterile instrument handling.
n.4: Wiping or limiting use does not restore sterility.
n.2: Lack of visible debris does not mean the file is suitable for reuse chairside.
n.0: A contaminated file should not be held for later clinical use.

Clinical Procedures.q: An anterior composite is being prepared and the operator asks for the conditioning gel. Which material is most commonly supplied as a phosphoric acid gel for enamel etching before composite bonding?
Clinical Procedures.w: Phosphoric acid etchant is routinely used to condition enamel before bonding.

n.0: Calcium hydroxide is a liner/base material.

n.1: Petroleum jelly is not an etchant.

Clinical Procedures.q: Using the image, item number 3 is most useful for which purpose?

n.2: Discarding holders is unrelated to the key preoperative check.
n.3: Folding an apron is not the main priority.
n.1: The exposure button is unrelated once imaging is complete.
n.4: Sensor sleeve status is not the main surgical check.

Clinical Procedures.q: During ultrasonic scaling, the patient reports sharp sensitivity. What is the best immediate response?

n.2: Increasing power may worsen discomfort.
n.0: Ignoring symptoms is inappropriate.
n.4: Suction remains important during scaling.
n.1: Continuous drying can increase sensitivity.

Clinical Procedures.q: While fitting a matrix system, the band keeps lifting away from the gingival margin as the retainer is tightened. What is the most likely interpretation?
o: The curing light intensity is too low
The local anaesthetic has not taken full effect
The matrix band is not properly adapted or positioned
The restorative material has begun to set too early
Clinical Procedures.w: If the band lifts from the gingival margin during tightening, it usually indicates poor adaptation or incorrect positioning of the matrix system.

n.1: Anaesthetic effectiveness does not determine whether a matrix band adapts correctly at the margin.
n.0: Curing light intensity is unrelated to how the matrix band fits before restoration placement.
n.4: Material setting would not usually explain loss of matrix adaptation before insertion of the material.
n.3: Patient movement may interfere with treatment, but repeated lifting during tightening mainly points to matrix adaptation problems.

Clinical Procedures.q: A temporary crown becomes loose shortly after cementation, and the cement mix had appeared very runny at the time of use. What is the most likely interpretation?
o: The crown must have had ideal retention form
The impression material used earlier was hydrophobic
The patient's bite was definitely balanced correctly
The polishing stage was carried out too late
The powder-liquid ratio may have been inaccurate
Clinical Procedures.w: A runny cement mix suggests an inaccurate powder-liquid ratio, which can reduce strength and retention of the temporary crown.

n.0: Ideal retention form would be less likely to result in early loosening if the cement were satisfactory.
n.2: Balanced occlusion alone does not explain why a temporary crown loosened shortly after cementation.
n.1: The earlier impression material does not explain the immediate properties of the cement mix at placement.
n.3: Polishing timing is not the likely reason for early loss of a crown with a visibly runny cement mix.

Clinical Procedures.q: During irrigation, sodium hypochlorite is accidentally drawn up into an unlabelled syringe on the tray. What is the best action?
o: Ask the operator to confirm what is in it before use
Discard it safely and replace it with a clearly identified syringe
Label the syringe now and continue using it
Set it aside for irrigation only at the end of the procedure
Use it for canal lubrication rather than irrigation
Clinical Procedures.w: Potentially hazardous irrigants must be clearly identified. An unlabelled syringe should be discarded safely and replaced appropriately.

n.0: Verbal confirmation does not meet the requirement for a labelled container.
n.2: Labelling after the fact records an assumption about the contents.
n.3: An unlabelled syringe left on the tray is precisely the hazard.
n.4: Hypochlorite is not a lubricant, and the contents are still unconfirmed.

Clinical Procedures.q: Composite remains soft after the normal curing cycle. What is the most likely interpretation?
o: The matrix band is too tight
The restoration may be inadequately cured
The tooth was polished too early
Clinical Procedures.w: A soft surface commonly indicates inadequate polymerisation or insufficient light delivery.

n.1: Matrix tightness does not cause uncured composite.
n.4: Polishing timing is not the likely cause of softness.
n.0: Shallow cavities usually cure more easily.
n.2: Fluoride varnish is unrelated.

n.3: A three-in-one syringe has a nozzle design.
