n.0: Air polishers have different attachments.

Clinical Procedures.q: After extraction, the patient asks when to remove the gauze pack. Best advice is usually to:
Clinical Procedures.w: Timing depends on the procedure and clinician instructions, commonly after a short pressure period.

n.2: Immediate removal may reduce clot support.
n.1: Two days is excessive and inappropriate.
n.3: Rinsing immediately may disturb clotting.
n.4: Sleeping with gauze in place may be unsafe.

Clinical Procedures.q: Using the image, what is the most likely purpose of item number 5?

n.2: Polishing requires a handpiece and polishing cup.
n.4: Impressions need trays and materials.
n.3: Pocket depths are recorded with a probe.
n.0: Cement mixing uses a pad and spatula.

Clinical Procedures.q: A posterior composite restoration still appears soft and slightly tacky after the normal curing cycle has been completed. What is the most likely interpretation?
o: The cavity preparation was too shallow
The matrix band was tightened too firmly
The patient has excessive salivary flow
The restoration may have been inadequately cured
The selected shade was too opaque for finishing
Clinical Procedures.w: A soft or tacky surface after curing suggests that polymerisation may be incomplete and the restoration may not have cured adequately.

n.1: Matrix tension influences contour and adaptation, not the curing status of the composite.
n.0: A shallow cavity would not normally explain a persistently soft cured surface.
n.2: Salivary flow can affect isolation but does not directly explain tackiness after curing.
n.4: Shade opacity can influence curing depth in some cases, but the direct interpretation here is inadequate curing rather than a finishing issue.

Clinical Procedures.q: Using the image, identify item number 3.

n.2: Torque drivers are associated with implants.

Clinical Procedures.q: Using the image, item number 1 is best described as:

Clinical Procedures.q: A composite restoration appears dull and tacky after curing. What is the most likely interpretation?

Clinical Procedures.q: A syringe of irrigant is passed without the side-vented needle requested by the operator. What is the most likely consequence if this goes unnoticed?

Working length will become electronically fixed

Clinical Procedures.q: The curing light tip is visibly coated with composite residue and is used without being cleaned. What is the most likely consequence?

Improved contact point formation in the proximal box
More accurate shade matching under the operating light
Reduced light transmission to the restoration surface

n.0: Etching is unrelated to contamination on the curing light tip.
n.2: Amalgam expansion is not influenced by whether the curing light tip is clean.
n.1: Contact point formation depends on matrixing and contour, not light-tip cleanliness.
n.3: A contaminated curing light tip does not improve shade matching and may reduce clinical effectiveness.

Clinical Procedures.q: Using the image, what is the most likely deposit shown around the cervical margins?

Clinical Procedures.q: An upper molar is to be removed under local anaesthetic. Which item is most appropriate for grasping and removing a tooth crown during routine extraction?
Clinical Procedures.w: Extraction forceps are designed to grip and remove teeth.

n.2: Needle holders are for suturing.
n.0: College tweezers handle small items.
n.4: Wax knives are laboratory instruments.

Clinical Procedures.q: During canal irrigation, the nurse notices that sodium hypochlorite has been drawn into an unlabelled syringe. What is the best action?
o: Dilute it with water so it becomes less hazardous
Discard it safely and replace it with a correctly identified syringe
Keep it separate and rely on memory to identify it
Pass it immediately before there is any confusion
Use it only for the first canal instrument pass
Clinical Procedures.w: A hazardous irrigant must be clearly identified. An unlabelled syringe should be discarded safely and replaced to reduce the risk of error.

n.2: Relying on memory is unsafe and creates avoidable risk in a clinical setting.
n.4: An unlabelled syringe should not be used for any stage of irrigation.
n.0: Dilution does not solve the problem of unsafe identification and may alter the intended concentration.
n.3: Using it quickly does not reduce the risk of misidentification or patient harm.

o: Occlusal contacts will become easier to establish

The restoration will become more resistant to moisture

n.0: Occlusal contact formation is not improved by destabilising the restoration early.
n.4: Moisture resistance does not increase because a matrix band is removed prematurely.

Clinical Procedures.q: A patient attends for a tooth-coloured restoration on an upper canine. Which material is commonly used to etch enamel before placement of a bonded composite restoration?
Clinical Procedures.w: Phosphoric acid gel is commonly used to etch enamel to improve micromechanical retention before bonding.

n.0: Calcium hydroxide is used as a lining material, particularly near the pulp, not for enamel etching.
n.3: Polycarboxylate is a luting or restorative cement, not an etching material.
n.1: Petroleum jelly is not used to create the etched enamel surface required for bonding.

n.3: Mixing time does not correct an incorrect powder-liquid ratio.

n.4: Risks should be discussed where relevant.
n.0: Patients should not be rushed.

Professionalism & Patient Care.q: A patient says they do not understand the aftercare instructions following an extraction. What is the best response?
o: Ask them to read the aftercare leaflet at home
Give the instructions again using the same wording
Rephrase the advice clearly and check understanding
Suggest they telephone the practice if problems arise
Write the instructions down for them to take away
Professionalism & Patient Care.w: Clear rephrasing and checking understanding supports safe, effective patient communication.

n.0: A leaflet supports the conversation but does not replace it.
n.1: Repetition of wording that did not work is unlikely to work now.
n.3: Useful safety net, but the aftercare needs understanding now.
n.4: Helpful and often done, but understanding should be confirmed first.

Professionalism & Patient Care.q: Someone telephones the practice asking about another person's treatment. Which situation is most likely to require careful identity checking before sharing information?
o: A caller requesting patient details by telephone
A cleaner asking where bins are stored
A colleague asking for tea orders
A patient requesting their own appointment time
Professionalism & Patient Care.w: Telephone requests for patient information require caution and appropriate verification.

n.4: A simple appointment request may still need checks, but detailed records requests carry higher risk.
n.1: Bin locations are not patient confidential data.
n.3: Supply deliveries are unrelated.
n.2: Tea orders are unrelated.

Professionalism & Patient Care.q: A patient telephones asking for details of their spouse's treatment plan. What is the best response?
o: Confirm the appointment date but no clinical detail
Explain that information cannot be shared without appropriate authority or consent
Give the details once identity has been verified
Provide the information as they are next of kin
Share only the outstanding balance on the account
Professionalism & Patient Care.w: Patient information should only be shared when there is appropriate consent, authority or another lawful basis.

n.0: Attendance is itself confidential.
n.2: Verifying who is calling does not give them a right to the information.
n.3: Spouses have no automatic entitlement to health information.
n.4: Financial information about a patient is also confidential.

Professionalism & Patient Care.q: A patient signs a form but says they do not understand the procedure. What is the best action?
o: Ask a colleague to witness the signature instead
Ask the patient to read the form again before starting
Note their comment in the records and proceed
Pause and ensure further explanation before treatment continues
Proceed as the signed form provides valid consent
Professionalism & Patient Care.w: A signature alone is not enough if the patient does not understand what they are consenting to.

n.0: A witness confirms the signature, not the understanding behind it.
n.1: Re-reading rarely resolves a misunderstanding that has been voiced.
n.2: Recording that consent was invalid does not make it valid.
n.4: A signature without understanding is not informed consent.

Professionalism & Patient Care.q: A patient accidentally overpays at reception and does not notice. What is the most ethical action?
o: Apply the overpayment as credit against future treatment
Hold the amount and refund it if the patient asks
Inform the patient and correct the payment
Record it in the day book and raise it at the month end
Refund it to the card without telling the patient
Professionalism & Patient Care.w: Ethical practice requires honesty, fairness and correcting financial errors promptly.

n.0: Decides on the patient's behalf what happens to their money.
n.1: Relies on the patient noticing an error that was ours.
n.3: Recording is right; the delay is not.
n.4: Corrects the money but leaves an unexplained transaction on their statement.

Professionalism & Patient Care.q: A patient is seated for an extraction and says they are unsure whether they want to continue. What is the best immediate action?
o: Ask the nurse to persuade the patient
Begin local anaesthetic quickly before they change their mind
Pause treatment and inform the dentist so the patient can discuss options
Proceed because the appointment was booked
Tell the patient they must continue
Professionalism & Patient Care.w: If a patient expresses uncertainty, treatment should pause so valid consent can be reviewed and the patient can decide freely.

n.3: A booking does not replace valid consent.
n.0: Patients should not be pressured into treatment.
n.1: Starting treatment without clear consent is inappropriate.
n.4: Patients cannot be forced to continue elective treatment.

Professionalism & Patient Care.q: A patient has arrived for a planned appointment and is waiting in reception. Which sequence best reflects good patient management when escorting someone into the surgery?
o: Ask for payment, then check name
Confirm identity, welcome them, explain what happens next
Leave them standing while preparing instruments
Seat them first, identify later, explain nothing
Professionalism & Patient Care.w: Checking identity, welcoming the patient and explaining the next steps supports safe, respectful care.

n.3: Identity should be confirmed before proceeding.
n.4: Treatment should not begin before appropriate introduction and checks.
n.0: Administrative matters do not replace identity checks.
n.2: Leaving patients unsupported may reduce confidence.

Professionalism & Patient Care.q: A colleague gives a patient conflicting appointment information. What is the best action?
o: Ask the patient which version they would prefer
Book the patient in again to be certain
Correct your colleague in front of the patient
Let the appointment stand and adjust the diary later
Professionalism & Patient Care.w: Prompt clarification prevents confusion and maintains confidence.

n.0: Preference does not establish what was actually arranged.
n.1: Creates a duplicate booking and more confusion.
n.3: Undermines the colleague and the patient's confidence.
n.4: Leaves the patient holding information you know to be wrong.

Professionalism & Patient Care.q: A patient arrives angry about a previous delay. What is the best first action?
o: Apologise and offer a goodwill gesture
Explain that delays are unavoidable in clinical practice
Explain what caused the delay on the previous visit
Listen calmly and acknowledge the frustration
Offer to move them to the front of today's list
Professionalism & Patient Care.w: Listening calmly and acknowledging concerns often helps de-escalate conflict.

n.0: An apology is right, but a gesture before listening can feel like being bought off.
n.1: Defends the practice rather than hearing the patient.
n.2: May be appropriate later, and may involve another patient's confidentiality.
n.4: Unfair to other patients and rewards the anger rather than resolving it.

Professionalism & Patient Care.q: A patient with hearing difficulty attends alone. What is the best approach?
o: Ask them to bring someone with them next time
Communicate mainly in writing to avoid misunderstanding
Face the patient and communicate clearly
Raise your voice slightly to make sure you are heard
Remove your mask whenever you speak to them
Professionalism & Patient Care.w: Facing the patient and speaking clearly can support lip reading and understanding.

n.0: Does nothing for today's appointment and reduces their independence.
n.1: A useful support, but not a substitute for direct communication.
n.3: Volume distorts speech; clarity and facing the patient help more.
n.4: Helps lip-reading, but only where infection control allows it.

Professionalism & Patient Care.q: A patient becomes upset at reception about waiting time. What is the best first response?
o: Acknowledge the frustration and speak calmly
Apologise and offer to rebook them for another day
Explain that the delay is caused by an emergency patient
Explain that the practice is running behind for everyone
Offer them a drink and ask them to take a seat
Professionalism & Patient Care.w: Acknowledging feelings calmly can de-escalate tension and open constructive discussion.

n.1: Jumps to a solution before the patient feels heard.
n.2: Reasonable context, but explanations land better after acknowledgement — and this may breach another patient's confidentiality.
n.3: Reads as a defence rather than a response.
n.4: A kind gesture that sidesteps what they have said.

Professionalism & Patient Care.q: A nurse is called away from reception while patient records are open on screen. Which action best supports confidentiality when leaving a computer workstation?
o: Ask a patient to watch the screen
Lock or log out of the screen
Professionalism & Patient Care.w: Locking or logging out helps prevent unauthorised access to patient information.

n.1: Open records may be viewed by others.
n.4: Visible passwords create security risks.
n.0: Patients should not supervise access to records.
n.3: Turning screens outward increases exposure risk.

Professionalism & Patient Care.q: A patient feels faint after standing up from the chair. What is the best response?
o: Advise them to sit quietly until they feel able to leave
Ask them to wait in reception until the feeling passes
Assist them safely and alert the clinician
Encourage them to stand slowly and take deep breaths
Offer a glass of water and continue with the turnaround
Professionalism & Patient Care.w: A patient who feels faint should be supported safely and the clinician informed promptly.

n.0: Sitting helps, but a patient feeling faint should not be left unsupervised.
n.1: Moves an unsteady patient away from the people who can help.
n.3: Sensible advice, but standing is what triggered it.
n.4: A kind gesture that leaves the patient effectively unattended.

Professionalism & Patient Care.q: A clinic is overbooked and appointments are being shortened. Which behaviour most increases communication mistakes in practice?
Professionalism & Patient Care.w: Rushed conversations often lead to missed details and misunderstanding.

n.0: Checking understanding helps prevent errors.
n.4: Polite use of names can improve rapport.
n.1: Careful listening reduces mistakes.
n.3: Summaries reinforce key information.

Professionalism & Patient Care.q: A nurse is explaining a scale and polish to a patient who is unfamiliar with dental terms. Which statement is the clearest example of avoiding jargon?
o: We need to assess the dentition comprehensively
We will clean around your teeth and gums today
You need prophylaxis and scaling today
Professionalism & Patient Care.w: Plain language improves patient understanding more than technical terminology.

n.2: This includes professional terms some patients may not know.
n.4: Abbreviations and jargon may confuse patients.
n.3: Technical terminology may be unclear.
n.0: Complex wording may reduce understanding.

Professionalism & Patient Care.q: A nervous patient begins to speak about a previous bad experience. What is the best initial response?
o: Explain that techniques have improved a great deal since then
Invite them to explain and listen calmly
Reassure them that the clinician is very experienced
Suggest they discuss it with the clinician instead
Tell them that many patients feel the same way
Professionalism & Patient Care.w: Inviting the patient to explain helps build trust and identify concerns affecting care.

n.0: Probably true, but it answers a fear the patient has not finished describing.
n.2: Reassurance offered before listening tends not to land.
n.3: Passes the patient on at the moment they have chosen to open up.
n.4: Normalising can help later, but it can also feel dismissive here.

Professionalism & Patient Care.q: A staff member leaves printed patient labels in a public area. How should printed patient information be handled?
o: Collected promptly and stored securely, then disposed of as confidential waste
Left at reception for the patient to collect on their way out
Placed in the recycling once the appointment has finished
Retained in the surgery until the end of the working week
Shredded only if the patient's full name appears on them
Professionalism & Patient Care.w: Patient labels contain identifiable information and should not be left where others can access them.

n.1: Leaves identifiable information in a public area.
n.2: Recycling is not confidential disposal.
n.3: Days of unsecured storage is the original problem.
n.4: Other details can identify a patient just as easily.

Professionalism & Patient Care.q: A treatment plan has been discussed and the patient has agreed to proceed. Why should consent discussions be documented appropriately?
o: To demonstrate the appointment length was justified
To provide a clear record of decisions and information shared
To reduce the time spent discussing options with patients
To satisfy the practice's insurance requirements
To support the treatment plan estimate given to the patient
Professionalism & Patient Care.w: Accurate records help show what was discussed, agreed and planned.

n.0: Time recording serves a different purpose entirely.
n.2: Documentation supports the discussion; it does not shorten it.
n.3: Insurers may require it, but the purpose is the patient's record of care.
n.4: Costs are recorded separately from the consent discussion.

Professionalism & Patient Care.q: A surgery is running behind and the pre-treatment conversation is cut short. Which behaviour most increases consent-related mistakes in practice?
Professionalism & Patient Care.w: Rushed discussions often lead to poor understanding and weak consent processes.

n.0: Checking understanding reduces mistakes.
n.4: Clear language supports valid consent.
n.1: Time to decide supports autonomy.
n.2: Careful records support good practice.

Professionalism & Patient Care.q: A patient is visibly tense as they sit in the dental chair. Which non-verbal behaviour is most likely to reassure an anxious patient?
Professionalism & Patient Care.w: Calm, attentive body language can help patients feel listened to and reassured.

n.2: Negative expressions may increase anxiety.
n.1: Phone use appears distracted.
n.3: Closed posture may seem unapproachable.
n.4: Leaving mid-conversation appears dismissive.

Professionalism & Patient Care.q: A patient is being given home-care advice at the end of an appointment. Which sequence best reflects effective communication when giving home-care advice?
o: Ask no questions and assume agreement
Explain clearly, invite questions, confirm understanding
Professionalism & Patient Care.w: Clear explanation, opportunities for questions and checking understanding support good outcomes.

n.3: Rushed explanations may be missed.
n.2: Leaflets alone may not be enough.
n.4: Starting with jargon may confuse patients.
n.0: Assumptions may hide misunderstanding.

Professionalism & Patient Care.q: A parent attends with a child for treatment. What should be recognised about consent?
o: Consent depends on age, capacity and legal authority under local rules
The accompanying parent can always consent for any child
The child can consent alone from the age of sixteen only
The dentist decides whether consent is needed in each case
Written consent from both parents is always required
Professionalism & Patient Care.w: Consent for children depends on the child's competence, age and who has authority to consent.

n.1: Only someone with parental responsibility can consent, which not every accompanying adult has.
n.2: A younger child with sufficient understanding may be able to consent.
n.3: Consent is always required; the question is who can give it.
n.4: One person with parental responsibility is generally sufficient.

Professionalism & Patient Care.q: A patient is due to begin a course of treatment and the consent form is being completed. Which statement best describes valid consent in dental care?
o: It can be given by any relative
It is given only in writing
It is only needed for surgical treatment
It is voluntary, informed and given by a person with capacity
Professionalism & Patient Care.w: Valid consent should be given freely, based on adequate information, by someone with capacity to decide.

n.1: Consent may be verbal, written or implied depending on circumstances.
n.4: Consent can be withdrawn and may need reconfirmation.
n.2: Consent applies to many forms of treatment, not only surgery.
n.0: Relatives cannot automatically consent for competent adults.

Professionalism & Patient Care.q: A practice regularly runs late and appointments are compressed. Which behaviour most increases patient management problems in practice?
Professionalism & Patient Care.w: Rushing patients often leads to anxiety, confusion and dissatisfaction.

n.1: Clear explanations usually improve management.
n.0: Checking comfort supports positive care.
n.2: Listening helps address issues early.
n.3: Organisation reduces avoidable problems.

Professionalism & Patient Care.q: A nurse discusses a patient's treatment loudly in the waiting room. What is the main concern?
Professionalism & Patient Care.w: Discussing patient information where others can hear may breach confidentiality.

n.4: Crowding is secondary to the privacy issue.
n.1: Timing is not the key concern.
n.3: Speaking clearly is not the issue.
n.2: Chair occupancy is irrelevant.

Professionalism & Patient Care.q: A team member posts about an unusual case they saw at work that day. Why should staff avoid discussing patients on social media, even without naming them?
o: Details may still identify the patient or breach trust
It may attract negative comments about the practice
It may breach the practice's social media policy
Posts about work should be made outside working hours
The practice owns any images taken on the premises
Professionalism & Patient Care.w: Seemingly anonymous details can still identify individuals and undermine confidentiality.

n.1: Reputation is secondary to the patient's confidentiality.
n.2: The policy exists because of the confidentiality risk.
n.3: Timing does not change the confidentiality issue.
n.4: Ownership is a separate matter.

Professionalism & Patient Care.q: Referral letters and laboratory sheets accumulate at reception during a busy clinic. Which sequence best reflects safe handling of confidential paperwork?
o: Collect it promptly, store securely, dispose of it appropriately when no longer needed
Collect it promptly, store securely, then archive every document indefinitely
File it at the end of the week and shred anything left over
Keep it on the desk while in use, then file it at the end of the day
Scan it immediately, then place the paper in the general waste
Professionalism & Patient Care.w: Confidential documents should be controlled, securely stored and disposed of through approved methods.

n.1: Keeping everything indefinitely conflicts with retention policy.
n.2: Leaves identifiable information unsecured for days.
n.3: A whole day on an open desk is a confidentiality risk.
n.4: The scanning is fine; general waste is the wrong disposal route.

Professionalism & Patient Care.q: A patient is hesitating about proceeding with an extraction. Which behaviour most undermines voluntary consent?
o: Allowing time for the patient to ask questions
Checking the patient has understood the options
Explaining the consequences of not proceeding
Pressuring the patient by saying they have no choice
Professionalism & Patient Care.w: Consent must be freely given without coercion or undue pressure.

n.0: Supports voluntary consent.
n.1: Supports informed consent.
n.2: Legitimate information, not pressure.
n.3: Widens choice rather than removing it.

Professionalism & Patient Care.q: A relative telephones asking what treatment a patient received. Which statement best describes confidentiality in dental practice?
o: It ends once treatment is complete
It is optional if the practice is busy
Patient information should be protected and shared only appropriately
Professionalism & Patient Care.w: Confidentiality requires protecting personal information and limiting disclosure to appropriate circumstances.

n.3: Many forms of patient information are confidential, not only notes.
n.0: It applies to all patients.
n.1: Duties continue after treatment ends.
n.2: Workload does not remove confidentiality duties.

Professionalism & Patient Care.q: Reception is busy and several conversations are taking place at once. Which behaviour most increases confidentiality mistakes in practice?
o: Checking who is present before speaking
Rushing and discussing patient details carelessly
Professionalism & Patient Care.w: Rushed and careless communication commonly leads to avoidable confidentiality breaches.

n.0: Awareness of who is present reduces risk.
n.1: Locking screens improves information security.
n.4: Secure disposal helps protect data.
n.3: Private, discreet discussion supports confidentiality.

Professionalism & Patient Care.q: A patient has been offered several options for restoring a broken molar. Which sequence best reflects a sound consent process for planned treatment?
o: Ask nurse only, start immediately, document later
Book appointment, take payment, begin treatment
Explain options and risks, answer questions, obtain agreement, record appropriately
Provide leaflet only, no discussion needed
Treat first, explain later, document if needed
Professionalism & Patient Care.w: Patients should receive information, have questions answered, then agree before treatment proceeds, with suitable records kept.

n.4: Explanation should come before treatment.
n.1: Payment and booking do not replace consent.
n.0: The clinician remains responsible for treatment discussions.
n.3: Leaflets may help but do not replace discussion.

Professionalism & Patient Care.q: A patient begins describing a problem they have had since their last visit. Which behaviour best demonstrates active listening?
o: Maintaining attention and responding to concerns
Professionalism & Patient Care.w: Active listening involves giving attention, acknowledging concerns and responding appropriately.

n.2: Interrupting can discourage patients from speaking.
n.3: Constant screen focus may reduce engagement.
n.1: Assuming the patient's words may be inaccurate.
n.0: Changing topic quickly may ignore concerns.

Professionalism & Patient Care.q: A patient attending for an extraction speaks very little English and has come alone. Which action best supports informed consent when a patient has limited English?
o: Ask a bilingual colleague to assist informally
Ask a family member to translate the discussion
Provide written information in English to read later
Use appropriate communication support such as an interpreter in line with policy
Use simple English and check understanding with teach-back
Professionalism & Patient Care.w: Patients need information they can understand, and suitable communication support may be necessary.

n.0: Well intentioned, but an untrained translator may omit or soften clinical detail.
n.1: Common in practice, but risks filtering of information and removes confidentiality.
n.2: Consent must be understood before treatment, not afterwards.
n.4: Good communication practice generally, but not sufficient on its own for informed consent.

Professionalism & Patient Care.q: A patient who is anxious about injections is having a restoration placed. Which approach best supports management of a nervous patient during treatment?
o: Explain every step in detail as it happens
Keep the appointment as short as possible
Play music to distract them from the procedure
Reassure them repeatedly throughout the treatment
Use calm communication and agreed pauses if needed
Professionalism & Patient Care.w: Calm communication and planned pauses can help anxious patients feel more in control.

n.0: Detail helps some patients and overwhelms others; agreeing a signal helps everyone.
n.1: Rushing tends to raise anxiety rather than reduce it.
n.2: A useful adjunct, but it does not give the patient any control.
n.3: Constant reassurance can draw attention to the thing being feared.

Professionalism & Patient Care.q: A patient nods and opens their mouth for a routine examination after explanation. What type of consent is this most likely to represent?
Professionalism & Patient Care.w: A patient's cooperative actions after explanation may indicate implied consent for simple routine procedures.

n.4: No written form is described.
n.3: No third party is involved.
n.2: Consent is not retrospective here.
n.1: The patient's actions indicate agreement.

Professionalism & Patient Care.q: A restoration is being placed when the patient raises a hand and becomes distressed. Which situation most clearly shows that consent may no longer be valid?
o: The patient asks how much longer it will take
The patient checks the cost partway through
The patient requests a break to rinse
The patient says they want to stop during treatment
The patient shifts position in the chair
Professionalism & Patient Care.w: Patients may withdraw consent at any time, including during treatment.

n.0: A reasonable question rather than a withdrawal.
n.1: Relates to the financial agreement, not consent to proceed.
n.2: A pause is not a withdrawal of consent.
n.4: Discomfort rather than a decision.

Professionalism & Patient Care.q: A patient asks to discuss their results where others are seated nearby. What is the best action?
o: Ask the patient to lower their voice while you talk
Continue quietly where you are so as not to make a fuss
Explain that results cannot be discussed at reception
Offer a more private area if possible
Offer to telephone the patient later that day instead
Professionalism & Patient Care.w: Sensitive discussions should take place in as private a setting as reasonably possible.

n.0: Places responsibility for confidentiality on the patient.
n.1: Quiet speech in a waiting area is still overheard.
n.2: True but unhelpfully blunt; offering an alternative is better.
n.4: A reasonable fallback, but only if no private space is available now.

Professionalism & Patient Care.q: A patient becomes increasingly anxious while waiting for treatment and says they may leave. What is the best immediate response?
o: Acknowledge the concern and inform the clinician promptly
Explain how much longer the wait is likely to be
Offer to rebook the appointment for another day
Reassure them that they will be seen very shortly
Sit with them until they are called through
Professionalism & Patient Care.w: Recognising anxiety, responding supportively and alerting the clinician can help manage the situation safely.

n.1: Useful information, but the clinician needs to know the patient may leave.
n.2: Accepts the loss of the appointment before trying to help them stay.
n.3: A promise you may not be able to keep.
n.4: Kind, but it keeps the clinician unaware of the situation.

Professionalism & Patient Care.q: A colleague asks you to record that sterilisation checks were completed, but you know they were missed. What is the most ethical response?
o: Ask the colleague to complete the record themselves
Complete the record but add a note of your concern
Record it and mention it to the manager next week
Refuse to record false information and raise the concern appropriately
Report it anonymously without speaking to anyone
Professionalism & Patient Care.w: Ethical behaviour requires honesty, accurate records and raising concerns about unsafe or false practices.

n.0: The entry would still be false; who writes it does not change that.
n.1: You would still be creating a knowingly false record.
n.2: Delays a patient-safety issue and the false entry stands in the meantime.
n.4: Raising concerns is right, but the false record must be refused first.

Professionalism & Patient Care.q: A patient who uses a wheelchair cannot access the first-floor surgery. What does the Equality Act 2010 require the practice to consider?
o: Asking the patient to attend a different practice
Making reasonable adjustments so the patient can be treated
Offering treatment only when a ground-floor room is free
Recording that the patient declined treatment
Treating the patient in the reception area
Professionalism & Patient Care.w: The Equality Act 2010 requires service providers to make reasonable adjustments so disabled people are not put at a substantial disadvantage.

n.0: Referring the problem elsewhere is not an adjustment.
n.2: Better than nothing, but the duty is to consider adjustments actively.
n.3: The patient has not declined; access has been denied.
n.4: Not a clinical environment and compromises privacy and infection control.

Professionalism & Patient Care.q: A patient with a learning disability attends for an examination and appears anxious. Which approach is most appropriate?
o: Ask their companion to answer all questions for them
Carry out the examination as quickly as possible
Give information in a way they can understand and involve them in decisions
Postpone treatment until a relative can attend
Speak mainly to the accompanying carer
Professionalism & Patient Care.w: Adults are presumed to have capacity; information should be given in an accessible form and the patient involved in decisions.

n.0: Assumes a lack of capacity that has not been established.
n.1: Speed increases anxiety and reduces understanding.
n.3: Delays care on an assumption about capacity.
n.4: The patient should be addressed directly wherever possible.

Professionalism & Patient Care.q: A patient living with dementia becomes distressed and confused during a long appointment. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Ask a colleague to hold the patient still
Continue quickly to finish before it worsens
Explain that they agreed to treatment earlier
Pause, reassure and consider shorter appointments in future
Proceed on the basis of the consent already signed
Professionalism & Patient Care.w: Consent is ongoing; distress means pausing, and future care should be adapted to the patient's needs.

n.0: Restraint is not an acceptable way to complete treatment.
n.1: Prioritises the procedure over the patient's distress.
n.2: Consent can be withdrawn at any point.
n.4: A signature does not override present distress or withdrawal.

Professionalism & Patient Care.q: A patient's first language is not English and no interpreter is available at short notice. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Ask a family member to translate the consent discussion
Postpone non-urgent treatment until interpreting support is arranged
Proceed using gestures and simple English
Provide a written consent form in English
Treat only if the patient signs the form
Professionalism & Patient Care.w: Valid consent requires understanding; non-urgent treatment should wait until proper interpreting support is available.

n.0: Common in practice, but risks filtering and removes confidentiality.
n.2: Insufficient for the understanding valid consent requires.
n.3: A form in a language they cannot read evidences nothing.
n.4: A signature without understanding is not valid consent.

Professionalism & Patient Care.q: A patient tells reception they are autistic and find waiting rooms overwhelming. Which adjustment is most appropriate?
o: Ask them to wait outside until called
Book them at a quieter time and reduce waiting where possible
Explain that all patients must wait their turn
Offer them a magazine to pass the time
Seat them in the busiest area so they are not forgotten
Professionalism & Patient Care.w: Reasonable adjustments include appointment timing and reducing sensory load in the waiting environment.

n.0: Excludes the patient rather than accommodating them.
n.2: Equal treatment is not the same as equitable treatment.
n.3: Does nothing about the sensory environment.
n.4: Directly worsens the difficulty described.

Professionalism & Patient Care.q: A practice is reviewing its equality and diversity policy with the team. Which of the following is a protected characteristic under the Equality Act 2010?
o: Length of registration with the practice
Professionalism & Patient Care.w: Religion or belief is one of the nine protected characteristics under the Equality Act 2010.

n.0: Not one of the protected characteristics in the Act.
n.1: A practice administrative matter.
n.2: Not protected, though it may correlate with other factors.
n.3: A scheduling preference rather than a characteristic.

Professionalism & Patient Care.q: A patient who is deaf attends alone and lip-reads. Which action best supports communication?
o: Ask them to return with someone who can hear
Face the patient and speak clearly at a normal pace
Raise your voice so they can hear over the equipment
Speak to the patient while turned towards the notes
Write everything down and avoid speaking
Professionalism & Patient Care.w: Facing the patient with clear, normally paced speech supports lip-reading; masks and turning away remove it.

n.0: Reduces the patient's independence and delays care.
n.2: Shouting distorts lip patterns and does not help.
n.3: Removes the visual information they rely on.
n.4: Writing supports communication but should not replace it.

Professionalism & Patient Care.q: A patient is given post-operative instructions at the end of a long appointment. Which technique best confirms they have understood?
o: Ask if they have any questions
Ask them to explain the instructions back in their own words
Give them a printed leaflet to take home
Repeat the instructions a second time
Write the instructions in the notes
Professionalism & Patient Care.w: Asking the patient to repeat the information back, sometimes called teach-back, is the reliable way to confirm understanding.

n.0: Most patients say no even when they have not understood.
n.2: Useful reinforcement, but it does not confirm understanding now.
n.3: Repetition does not test whether they were understood.
n.4: Records what was said, not what was understood.

Professionalism & Patient Care.q: A nervous patient is talking rapidly about their fears while the surgery is being prepared. Which response best demonstrates active listening?
o: Carry on preparing and reply when finished
Nod occasionally while continuing to set up
Reassure them that there is nothing to worry about
Stop, face the patient and acknowledge what they have said
Tell them the appointment will be over quickly
Professionalism & Patient Care.w: Active listening means giving full attention and reflecting back what has been heard before responding.

n.0: Delays the response and signals that the task matters more.
n.1: Gives the appearance of listening without the substance.
n.2: Dismisses a fear that has not yet been heard.
n.4: Focuses on ending the experience rather than understanding it.

Professionalism & Patient Care.q: A patient telephones asking whether their relative attended an appointment. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Confirm attendance but give no clinical detail
Confirm only if the caller knows the date of birth
Explain that patient information cannot be shared without consent
Give the information if the relative is elderly
Transfer the call to the treating dentist
Professionalism & Patient Care.w: Whether a patient attended is confidential; it cannot be disclosed without the patient's consent.

n.0: Attendance is itself confidential patient information.
n.1: Identity checks confirm who is calling, not their right to the information.
n.3: Age does not remove a patient's right to confidentiality.
n.4: Passes the problem on without resolving the confidentiality issue.

Professionalism & Patient Care.q: A patient becomes tearful while describing a previous painful experience. Which response is most appropriate?
o: Acknowledge how difficult that sounds and ask what would help today
Explain that dentistry has changed a great deal since then
Offer to rebook the appointment for another day
Reassure them that this dentist is very gentle
Suggest they try not to think about it
Professionalism & Patient Care.w: Acknowledging the feeling and asking what would help puts the patient in control of how care proceeds.

n.1: True, but it answers a fear before it has been heard.
n.2: Avoids the conversation rather than supporting the patient.
n.3: Reassurance offered before listening rarely lands.
n.4: Dismissive and unhelpful.

Professionalism & Patient Care.q: A dental nurse must explain an aftercare instruction to a patient with limited health literacy. Which approach is most effective?
o: Give a detailed explanation covering every eventuality
Provide the standard leaflet without comment
Speak more slowly using the same clinical terms
Use short sentences, plain words and check understanding
Write the instructions in full clinical detail
Professionalism & Patient Care.w: Plain language, short sentences and a check of understanding are the core of accessible health information.

n.0: Volume of information reduces what is retained.
n.1: A leaflet alone assumes reading confidence the patient may not have.
n.2: Pace does not make unfamiliar words understandable.
n.4: Detail is not the same as clarity.

Professionalism & Patient Care.q: A patient asks a question just as the dentist begins treatment. Which action best supports good communication?
o: Answer briefly while the treatment continues
Ask the dentist to pause so the question can be answered
Explain that questions should have been asked earlier
Ignore it so the treatment is not interrupted
Tell the patient it will be answered afterwards
Professionalism & Patient Care.w: A question raised during treatment may indicate uncertainty about consent, so it should be addressed at the time.

n.0: A partial answer during treatment can increase anxiety.
n.2: Discourages the patient from raising anything else.
n.3: An unanswered question may mean consent is in doubt.
n.4: Consent is ongoing; a question during treatment may signal hesitation.

Professionalism & Patient Care.q: A patient is visibly tense as the surgery is prepared around them. Which non-verbal behaviour is most likely to increase a patient's anxiety in the surgery?
o: Explaining each step before it happens
Making brief eye contact when speaking
Preparing instruments within the patient's view
Sitting at the patient's eye level
Speaking in a calm and unhurried tone
Professionalism & Patient Care.w: Visible instruments are a common anxiety trigger; preparation is best carried out out of the patient's line of sight.

n.0: Predictability reduces anxiety for most patients.
n.1: Supports rapport rather than undermining it.
n.3: Reduces the sense of being loomed over.
n.4: Actively calming.

Professionalism & Patient Care.q: A patient with limited English nods and smiles throughout an explanation but answers no questions. What should this suggest?
o: Their agreement is clear and treatment may proceed
They are content and no further checks are needed
They may not have understood and this should be checked
They prefer not to be spoken to directly
They wish the appointment to end quickly
Professionalism & Patient Care.w: Nodding and smiling without engaging with questions is a common sign that information has not been understood.

n.0: Nodding is often politeness rather than comprehension.
n.1: Contentment is not the same as understanding.
n.3: An assumption unsupported by the behaviour described.
n.4: Possible, but it does not address the consent problem.

Professionalism & Patient Care.q: Reception is busy and a patient asks about their treatment while others are waiting. Why should a dental nurse avoid discussing a patient's treatment in the reception area?
o: It may be overheard and breaches confidentiality
Reception staff are not clinically trained
The patient may forget what was said
Professionalism & Patient Care.w: Clinical discussions in public areas risk being overheard, which breaches the patient's confidentiality.

n.0: A practical concern, not the principal one.
n.2: True but not why the conversation is inappropriate.
n.3: A minor issue compared with confidentiality.
n.4: Recall is not the reason the setting is unsuitable.

Professionalism & Patient Care.q: A patient who is blind attends for treatment. Which approach best supports them in the surgery?
o: Ask a colleague to guide them by the arm without asking
Describe the room and explain each step before it happens
Give written information for them to read later
Use touch alone to direct them into position
Professionalism & Patient Care.w: Verbal description and warning before each step gives a blind patient the information sighted patients get visually.

n.0: Guidance should be offered and accepted, not imposed.
n.2: Standard print is inaccessible; alternative formats are needed.
n.3: The patient should be addressed directly.
n.4: Touch without explanation is disorientating.

Professionalism & Patient Care.q: A patient becomes angry and raises their voice in the surgery. What is the most appropriate initial response?
o: Continue treatment and ignore the outburst
Match their tone so they know you are serious
Remain calm, listen and acknowledge their concern
Warn them that the police will be called
Professionalism & Patient Care.w: De-escalation begins with staying calm, listening and acknowledging the concern before any other action.

n.0: May be necessary later, but not before attempting to de-escalate.
n.1: Ignoring anger usually intensifies it.
n.2: Escalates rather than resolves.
n.4: A last resort where there is a threat, not a first response.

Professionalism & Patient Care.q: A dental nurse must give instructions to a patient wearing a face covering in a noisy surgery. What is most likely to aid understanding?
o: Give the instructions while equipment is running
Reduce background noise and check understanding afterwards
Speak faster to finish before the next patient
Write nothing down so the patient concentrates
Professionalism & Patient Care.w: Reducing competing noise and checking understanding are more effective than raising volume.

n.0: Competing noise is a major barrier.
n.2: Volume does not overcome a noisy environment or a muffled voice.
n.3: Speed reduces comprehension.
n.4: Written backup supports rather than distracts.

Professionalism & Patient Care.q: A parent answers on behalf of a competent teenage patient throughout the appointment. What is the most appropriate approach?
o: Accept the parent's answers as they hold responsibility
Address the young person directly and involve them in decisions
Ask the parent to wait outside without discussion
Continue and record the parent as the decision maker
Refuse to treat unless the young person speaks
Professionalism & Patient Care.w: A young person with capacity should be addressed directly and involved in decisions about their own care.

n.0: A competent young person can make their own decisions.
n.2: May be appropriate but should be handled sensitively.
n.3: Records a decision maker who may not be the right one.
n.4: Disproportionate and unhelpful.

Professionalism & Patient Care.q: A colleague reading a set of notes cannot work out what a previous entry means. Why should abbreviations be used carefully in clinical records?
o: Abbreviations are prohibited in dental records
They make records harder to store electronically
They may be misread by others relying on the record
They reduce the professional appearance of notes
They take longer to write than full words
Professionalism & Patient Care.w: Records are read by others, sometimes years later; ambiguous abbreviations risk misinterpretation of care.

n.0: Agreed abbreviations are commonly used.
n.1: Storage is unaffected.
n.3: Appearance is not the concern.
n.4: They are quicker, which is why they are used.

Professionalism & Patient Care.q: A transgender patient's records show a name they no longer use. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Ask the patient how they wish to be addressed and update the record
Continue using the recorded name until documents are provided
Explain that records cannot be changed
Use the recorded name in front of other patients
Use whichever name the patient's referral shows
Professionalism & Patient Care.w: Patients should be asked how they wish to be addressed, and the record updated to reflect it.

n.1: Documentation is not required to record a preferred name.
n.2: Records can and should reflect the patient accurately.
n.3: Discloses information the patient may not wish shared.
n.4: The patient is the authority on their own name.

Professionalism & Patient Care.q: A practice is reviewing whether its service is accessible. Which action best identifies barriers patients face?
o: Ask patients about their experience and act on the feedback
Assume the building is compliant because it is modern
Compare the practice with others locally
Rely on the absence of complaints
Review the accessibility policy document alone
Professionalism & Patient Care.w: Barriers are best identified by asking the people who encounter them and acting on what is said.

n.1: Modern buildings can still present barriers.
n.2: Others may be equally inaccessible.
n.3: People who cannot access a service often do not complain, they go elsewhere.
n.4: A policy describes intention, not experience.

Professionalism & Patient Care.q: A patient requires a longer appointment because of a disability. How should this be viewed?
o: A cost the patient should meet
A favour the practice may extend if convenient
A reasonable adjustment supporting equal access
An exception requiring approval from the GDC
An unnecessary use of clinical time
Professionalism & Patient Care.w: Additional time is a common reasonable adjustment under the Equality Act, supporting equal access to care.

n.0: Patients cannot be charged for an adjustment.
n.1: Adjustments are a duty, not a courtesy.
n.3: The GDC has no role in individual appointment planning.
n.4: Time that enables treatment is not wasted.

Professionalism & Patient Care.q: A patient has been given a treatment plan with several options and costs. Which action best supports an informed decision?
o: Advise them which option most patients choose
Ask them to decide before leaving the surgery
Explain the options, risks and costs and give time to consider
Recommend the option the practice prefers
Suggest the cheapest option to avoid difficulty
Professionalism & Patient Care.w: Informed consent requires the options, risks and costs to be explained, with time to consider them.

n.0: What others choose is not a basis for this patient's decision.
n.1: Pressure to decide undermines voluntariness.
n.3: Introduces a conflict of interest.
n.4: Cost is one factor among several.

Professionalism & Patient Care.q: A patient asks why so many questions about their medical history are needed. What is the best explanation?
o: It allows the practice to charge correctly
It helps identify anything that could affect their treatment safely
It is a legal requirement with no clinical purpose
It is needed for the practice's insurance
It is routine paperwork completed for every patient
Professionalism & Patient Care.w: Medical history identifies conditions and medicines that may affect the safety of treatment.

n.0: Charging is unrelated to medical history.
n.2: The purpose is clinical, not administrative.
n.3: Insurance is not why the history is taken.
n.4: True but unhelpful; it does not explain why.

Professionalism & Patient Care.q: A patient does not attend several appointments and the practice wishes to contact them. What must be considered?
o: Contact may be made in any way that reaches them quickly
Contact should be made through a family member
Contact should follow the patient's stated preference and protect confidentiality
Messages may be left with anyone answering the telephone
The practice may discuss it with their employer
Professionalism & Patient Care.w: Contact arrangements should follow the patient's recorded preference and avoid disclosure to third parties.

n.0: Speed does not override confidentiality.
n.1: Third parties should not be used without consent.
n.3: Risks disclosure to someone with no right to it.
n.4: An employer has no entitlement to the information.

Professionalism & Patient Care.q: A patient asks for a copy of their dental records. What is the correct position?
o: Only a summary may ever be provided
Patients have a right of access to their records
Patients may see records only in the presence of the dentist
Records belong to the practice and cannot be released
Records may be released only to another dentist
Professionalism & Patient Care.w: Patients have a right to access their own health records under data protection law.

n.0: Access covers the record, not just a summary.
n.2: Supervised viewing is not a condition of access.
n.3: The practice holds them, but the patient has a right of access.
n.4: Access is the patient's right, not limited to professionals.

Professionalism & Patient Care.q: A patient who has difficulty reading is given a written consent form. What is the most appropriate approach?
o: Ask a relative to read and sign it for them
Ask them to take it home and return it signed
Explain it verbally, check understanding and record how consent was obtained
Provide a longer form with more detail
Read it aloud quickly and ask them to sign
Professionalism & Patient Care.w: Where reading is a barrier, consent is discussed verbally, understanding checked, and the method recorded.

n.0: A relative cannot consent for a competent adult.
n.1: Does not address the reading difficulty.
n.3: More text makes the barrier worse.
n.4: Speed prevents understanding.

Professionalism & Patient Care.q: A patient becomes distressed and asks for treatment to stop partway through. What must happen?
o: Continue as consent was given at the start
Continue to a safe stopping point and then stop
Stop immediately regardless of the stage of treatment
Stop only if the dentist agrees it is convenient
Professionalism & Patient Care.w: Consent can be withdrawn at any time; treatment stops at the earliest point that is safe for the patient.

n.0: Consent may be withdrawn at any time.
n.1: Ignores the withdrawal of consent.
n.3: Withdrawal must be respected, but stopping mid-procedure can itself be unsafe; the aim is the earliest safe point.
n.4: Convenience does not determine whether consent stands.

Professionalism & Patient Care.q: A patient is due to be seen by a different clinician at their next visit. Which record entry best supports continuity of care after an appointment?
o: A note of the time the appointment finished
A note that the patient attended
The name of the nurse assisting
What was done, what was advised and what is planned next
Whether the patient paid on the day
Professionalism & Patient Care.w: Records support continuity when they capture the treatment given, the advice provided and the plan going forward.

n.0: Administrative detail.
n.1: Attendance alone tells the next clinician nothing.
n.2: Useful for traceability, not for continuity of care.
n.4: A financial record, held separately.

Professionalism & Patient Care.q: A patient asks how much their treatment will cost before agreeing to it. What must they be given?
o: A written treatment plan and estimate of costs
Only the cost of today's appointment
The cost after treatment has been completed
Professionalism & Patient Care.w: Patients should receive a written treatment plan with an estimate of costs before agreeing to treatment.

n.0: Verbal figures are easily misremembered and disputed.
n.2: The patient needs the cost of the plan they are agreeing to.
n.3: Too late to inform the decision.
n.4: A price list is not a plan for this patient.

Professionalism & Patient Care.q: A patient's relative asks to sit in during the appointment. What determines whether this is acceptable?
o: Whether the relative has attended before
Whether there is space in the surgery
Professionalism & Patient Care.w: Anyone additional in the surgery is there with the patient's consent, which can be withdrawn.

n.0: Policy sets the framework, but the patient decides.
n.1: The clinician may raise practical concerns but does not decide alone.
n.3: Past attendance does not create ongoing permission.
n.4: A practical constraint, not the deciding factor.

Professionalism & Patient Care.q: A patient tells the dental nurse something in confidence and asks them not to tell the dentist. What is the correct approach?
o: Agree and keep the information private
Explain that clinically relevant information must be shared with the team
Share it with the whole practice team
Tell the dentist without saying anything to the patient
Professionalism & Patient Care.w: Confidentiality is not absolute within the team; the patient should be told what needs to be shared and why.

n.0: May withhold information that affects safe treatment.
n.2: A record nobody reads does not protect the patient.
n.3: Sharing should be limited to those who need to know.
n.4: Sharing may be necessary, but the patient should know it will happen.

Professionalism & Patient Care.q: A patient does not speak during the appointment and avoids eye contact. What is the most appropriate interpretation?
o: They are satisfied with the explanation given
They do not wish to receive treatment
They may be anxious, in pain or finding communication difficult
Professionalism & Patient Care.w: Withdrawal and avoided eye contact commonly indicate anxiety, pain or a communication barrier, and should be explored.

n.0: Attributes intent without evidence.
n.1: Silence is not agreement.
n.2: An assumption that should be checked rather than presumed.
n.3: Silence gives no evidence of understanding.

Professionalism & Patient Care.q: A dental nurse notices a patient's medical history has not been updated for three years. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Ask the patient to confirm and update it before treatment
Leave it for the dentist to notice
Update it only if the patient mentions something
Professionalism & Patient Care.w: Medical history is confirmed with the patient before treatment, not assumed to be unchanged.

n.1: Medicines and conditions change frequently.
n.2: Creates a false record of a current check.
n.3: Checking the history is part of preparing the patient.
n.4: Patients often do not know what is relevant.

Professionalism & Patient Care.q: A patient with anxiety asks to agree a signal to pause treatment. How should this be handled?
o: Agree a clear signal and confirm the team will stop when it is used
Agree but explain it can only be used between stages
Explain that stopping midway is not possible
Suggest they simply speak up if needed
Tell them the appointment is too short for pauses
Professionalism & Patient Care.w: An agreed stop signal gives an anxious patient control, and it only works if the team honours it.

n.1: Undermines the sense of control the signal is meant to give.
n.2: Treatment can almost always be paused at a safe point.
n.3: Speaking is difficult with instruments in the mouth.
n.4: Time pressure is not the patient's problem to absorb.

Professionalism & Patient Care.q: A patient asks a question the dental nurse does not know the answer to. What is the best response?
o: Answer as best they can from general knowledge
Explain they will find out and come back to them
Say the question is not important
Tell the patient nobody knows the answer
Professionalism & Patient Care.w: Saying you will find out is honest, maintains trust and ensures the patient gets accurate information.

n.0: Risks giving inaccurate information the patient will act on.
n.2: Dismisses a concern the patient has raised.
n.3: Passes responsibility to the patient and risks poor information.
n.4: Untrue and unhelpful.

Professionalism & Patient Care.q: A patient becomes upset when told the cost of treatment. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Acknowledge their concern and go through the plan and options again
Explain that the fees are fixed and cannot be changed
Offer to reduce the cost to resolve the situation
Suggest they postpone treatment until they have saved
Professionalism & Patient Care.w: Acknowledging the reaction and revisiting the plan and options helps the patient make an informed choice.

n.1: Closes the conversation without exploring alternatives.
n.2: Not the nurse's decision, and it avoids the real discussion.
n.3: Dismissive of a patient who may simply need the options explained.
n.4: Premature; a different option may suit them better.

Professionalism & Patient Care.q: A dental nurse is asked to translate for a patient because they speak the same language. What should be considered?
o: They may assist only if the patient is unaccompanied
They should agree, as it saves arranging an interpreter
They should decline all involvement in communication
Whether they are competent to interpret clinical information accurately
Whether they have time before the next patient
Professionalism & Patient Care.w: Speaking a language is not the same as being able to interpret clinical information accurately for consent.

n.0: Companionship is not the relevant test.
n.1: Convenience does not make interpretation accurate.
n.2: They may help with simple communication.
n.4: Time is not the professional consideration.

Professionalism & Patient Care.q: A patient with a physical disability asks how they will transfer to the dental chair. What is the best approach?
o: Ask the patient how they usually transfer and what help they want
Ask two staff to lift the patient across
Explain that treatment must happen in the wheelchair
Move them without discussion to save time
Tell them to bring someone to assist next time
Professionalism & Patient Care.w: The patient is the expert in their own transfer; asking first is both safer and more respectful.

n.1: Lifting without assessment risks injury to everyone.
n.2: Sometimes appropriate, but only after discussing it.
n.3: Removes the patient's control over their own body.
n.4: Places the burden on the patient.

Professionalism & Patient Care.q: A patient asks the dental nurse whether their treatment was carried out properly. What is the best response?
o: Confirm that it was, to reassure them
Encourage them to discuss it with the dentist and offer to arrange that
Explain that nurses cannot comment on anything
Give an opinion based on what they observed
Tell them to make a formal complaint
Professionalism & Patient Care.w: Questions about the quality of treatment belong with the clinician; the nurse's role is to facilitate that conversation.

n.0: Offers a clinical judgement the nurse is not able to give.
n.2: Unhelpfully absolute and leaves the patient unsupported.
n.3: Assisting is not assessing.
n.4: Escalates a question that may only need a conversation.

Professionalism & Patient Care.q: A patient attending for the first time is shown into the surgery. Why should a dental nurse introduce themselves and explain their role to a new patient?
o: It allows the patient to choose a different nurse
It builds trust and helps the patient know who is involved in their care
It is needed for the practice's records
It is required before consent can be signed
Professionalism & Patient Care.w: Introductions establish who is present and why, which supports trust and the patient's sense of control.

n.0: Not the purpose of an introduction.
n.2: Records note who assisted, but that is not the reason.
n.3: Introductions are good practice but not a formal consent requirement.
n.4: It takes a moment and does not shorten anything.

Professionalism & Patient Care.q: A patient discloses that they are frightened of needles just before an injection. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Continue quickly so it is over sooner
Explain that the injection is essential and proceed
Inform the operator and discuss options with the patient
Suggest they close their eyes and say nothing further
Tell the patient most people feel the same
Professionalism & Patient Care.w: A disclosure of fear should be shared with the operator so options can be discussed before proceeding.

n.0: Ignores a disclosure that may affect consent.
n.1: Removes the patient's choice.
n.3: A coping suggestion that leaves the operator unaware.
n.4: Normalising can feel dismissive when said instead of acting.

Professionalism & Patient Care.q: A patient asks that messages are not left on their home telephone. What is the main reason for recording a patient's preferred method of contact?
o: It allows marketing to be targeted
It ensures communication reaches them without breaching confidentiality
It is needed for appointment reminders only
It reduces the practice's postage costs
Professionalism & Patient Care.w: Recording contact preference means messages reach the patient by a route they consider private.

n.0: Marketing requires separate consent and is not the reason.
n.2: Reminders are one use among several.
n.3: A commercial side effect.
n.4: Efficiency is not the primary purpose.

Professionalism & Patient Care.q: A patient refuses a recommended radiograph. What should happen?
o: Explain that treatment cannot continue at all
Explain the reasons and consequences, respect the decision and record it
Proceed since the dentist has already decided
Take the radiograph at the next visit without discussion
Professionalism & Patient Care.w: A competent patient may refuse; the reasons and consequences are explained, the decision respected and recorded.

n.0: Overstates the position in most cases.
n.2: A recommendation is not consent.
n.3: Judgemental and inaccurate; a refusal is a valid choice.
n.4: Consent is required each time.

Professionalism & Patient Care.q: A patient's notes contain an abbreviation nobody in the practice recognises. What is the safest action?
o: Ask the author what it means before relying on it
Copy it forward into the new entry
Ignore it and continue with treatment
Professionalism & Patient Care.w: Ambiguous entries should be clarified with the author rather than guessed at or perpetuated.

n.1: Assumption in a clinical record risks acting on the wrong information.
n.2: Propagates an ambiguity.
n.3: Records are not deleted.
n.4: The entry may be clinically important.

Professionalism & Patient Care.q: A dental nurse is asked to describe what makes consent 'voluntary'. Which statement is most accurate?
o: It is given after a written form has been signed
It is given by someone with capacity
It is given once the treatment has been explained
It is given only for routine treatment
It is given without pressure from staff, family or others
Professionalism & Patient Care.w: Valid consent must be voluntary, informed and given by someone with capacity; voluntary means free from pressure.

n.0: A signature is evidence, not what makes consent voluntary.
n.1: Capacity is a separate element of valid consent.
n.2: That describes it being informed, not voluntary.
n.3: Voluntariness applies to all treatment.

Professionalism & Patient Care.q: A patient who has capacity makes a decision the team believes is unwise. What follows?
o: The decision may be overruled by the dentist
The patient must be assessed as lacking capacity
The patient should be discharged from the practice
Treatment should proceed in their best interests
Professionalism & Patient Care.w: A person with capacity is entitled to make decisions others consider unwise.

n.0: Clinicians advise; competent patients decide.
n.2: An unwise decision is not evidence of incapacity.
n.3: Disagreement is not grounds for discharge.
n.4: Best interests applies only where capacity is lacking.

Professionalism & Patient Care.q: A dental nurse is asked to witness that a patient has been given a treatment plan. What should they check?
o: That the patient has read every word
That the plan is signed by two clinicians
That the plan is the shortest option available
That the plan matches the practice's price list
That the plan was given and the patient had the chance to ask questions
Professionalism & Patient Care.w: The witness confirms the plan was provided and that the patient had an opportunity to ask questions.

n.0: Not something a witness can verify.
n.1: Not a requirement.
n.2: Length is not a measure of appropriateness.
n.3: Costs may legitimately vary by case.

Professionalism & Patient Care.q: A patient asks why they must repeat their medical history at every course of treatment. What is the best explanation?
o: It allows the practice to update its marketing list
It ensures the correct fee is charged
It is a formality with no clinical purpose
It is required by the practice's insurer
Their health and medicines may have changed since last time
Professionalism & Patient Care.w: Conditions and medicines change, and both can affect the safety of dental treatment.

n.0: Marketing is unrelated and requires separate consent.
n.1: Charging is unaffected by medical history.
n.2: The purpose is entirely clinical.
n.3: Insurers do not set the clinical requirement.

Professionalism & Patient Care.q: A dental nurse is asked to explain confidentiality to a new colleague. Which statement is most accurate?
o: Information may be shared freely within the practice
Information may be shared once treatment is complete
Information may be shared only with those who need it for the patient's care
Information may be shared with anyone who asks politely
Information may never be shared with anyone
Professionalism & Patient Care.w: Patient information is shared on a need-to-know basis with those involved in the patient's care.

n.0: Even within a team, sharing is on a need-to-know basis.
n.1: Confidentiality does not expire.
n.3: Manner of asking confers no entitlement.
n.4: Sharing within the care team is necessary and expected.

Professionalism & Patient Care.q: A patient asks the dental nurse to keep their diagnosis from a family member who attends with them. What should happen?
o: Discuss it in front of the family member anyway
Explain the practice cannot control what is said
Record the patient's wishes and respect them
Refuse, as families should be informed
Tell the family member privately afterwards
Professionalism & Patient Care.w: A competent patient decides who is told; their wishes should be recorded and followed.

n.0: Overrides the patient's explicit wish.
n.1: The practice can and must control its own disclosures.
n.3: Families have no automatic entitlement to information.
n.4: A deliberate breach of confidentiality.

Professionalism & Patient Care.q: A patient tells the nurse they did not understand what the dentist said but does not want to seem difficult. What is the best response?
o: Explain the treatment in the nurse's own words
Offer to ask the dentist to go over it again
Reassure them that the dentist knows best
Suggest they read about it at home
Tell them it is normal not to follow everything
Professionalism & Patient Care.w: Understanding is essential to consent; the nurse facilitates a further explanation rather than substituting one.

n.0: Risks introducing error and goes beyond the nurse's role.
n.2: Undermines the patient's right to understand their own care.
n.3: Leaves consent unresolved now.
n.4: Normalises a gap in understanding that affects consent.

Professionalism & Patient Care.q: A patient declines a radiograph the dentist has recommended. Why should a dental nurse record a patient's refusal of treatment as well as their agreement?
o: It allows the practice to charge a cancellation fee
It demonstrates the patient was difficult
It evidences that the discussion took place and the decision was informed
It is required before the patient can be discharged
It reduces the practice's liability entirely
Professionalism & Patient Care.w: Recording a refusal shows the options and consequences were explained and the patient made an informed choice.

n.0: Charging is unrelated to a clinical refusal.
n.1: Records are not for characterising patients.
n.3: Refusal is not grounds for discharge.
n.4: Records support good care; they do not remove liability.

Professionalism & Patient Care.q: A patient asks whether the dental nurse will be present throughout their treatment. What is the best response?
o: Explain that nurses move between surgeries as needed
Explain the nurse's role and that they will be present to assist
Say it depends how busy the practice is
Tell them it is not something patients usually ask
Tell them the dentist decides who is present
Professionalism & Patient Care.w: Explaining who will be present and what they do addresses a common source of patient anxiety.

n.0: Unsettling and does not answer the concern behind the question.
n.2: Suggests care depends on workload.
n.3: Dismissive of a legitimate concern.
n.4: Deflects a reasonable question.

Professionalism & Patient Care.q: A dental nurse is asked what should happen if a patient's details are sent to the wrong address. Which action comes first?
o: Amend the address and take no further action
Contact the recipient and ask them to destroy it
Report it as a data breach under the practice procedure
Tell the patient only if they ask
Wait to see whether any harm results
Professionalism & Patient Care.w: Disclosure of personal data to the wrong recipient is a data breach and follows the practice's reporting procedure.

n.0: Corrects the cause but ignores the breach that occurred.
n.1: Sensible mitigation, but reporting comes first.
n.3: Patients should be told where their data has been compromised.
n.4: Breach reporting is time-limited and does not wait on harm.
